REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON BANKING AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
In the absence of the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) I beg to present the eleventh report of the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce as follows:
Your committee have had under consideration the order of reference from this honourable House, dated 31st March, 1924 which reads as follows:-
That, in the opinion of this House, in view of the failure of the Home Bank, and of the fact that official prosecutions and inquiries have been instituted, including the Royal Commission which has been appointed to investigate the facts alleged in the petition represented by the depositors of the bank and the affairs of the bank generally; and considering that the evidence received and to be taken before the several tribunals will be available for consideration, the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce should be instructed to consider the provisions of the Bank Act with a view to recommending such amendments to the act as will better protect the interests of depositors generally and will prevent similar occurrences in the future; and also to consider the report of the Royal Commission in its bearing upon these matters and with respect to the possiblity of saving the Home Bank depositors from loss," be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce for such action as the committee may deem advisable.
And also the order of reference dated 11th June, 1924, reading as follows:-
"That the Interim Report of the Royal Commission respecting the Home Bank be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce."
Your committee have sat from time to time, and
244i
have studied the interim report on the Home Bank submitted by Mr. Chief Justice McKeown and the evidence therein referred to.
Your committee consider that the facts therein brought out and the evidence therein referred to clearly establish that the depositors of the Home Bank have no claim under the law the land for compensation by the country on account of any loss they may suffeT by reason of the failure of the Home Bank.
But your committee are also of the opinion that in view of the representations made to the Departmenl of Finance in the years 1916 and 1918, the government of the time could have made in 1916 and in 191 an effective audit under Section 56-A of the Bank Act and if such an effective audit or thorough investiga* tion into the bank's affairs had been made it would have resulted:-
1.	In the immediate liquidation of the bank, or
2. Its amalgamation with another bank, and that the effect yould have been, no loss to the depositors in 1916 or 1918.
Your committee have studied the evidence given before the Royal Commission by Sir Thomas White, who was then Minister of Finance, and particularly his statements: "I would never think of putting in a special auditor in a bank and taking chances, especially at a time like that, of closing the bank," (page 345); and further: "Under no circumstances would I have allowed a bank to fail during the period in question. I had many difficult and dangerous financial situations to deal with during the war. At its outbreak, in view of the panic which prevailed, the government, at my instance, placed itself behind the banks of Canada and gave public assurance that it would loan them such sums as they might require to meet the conditions of the war, and would take all further steps necessary to safeguard the financial situation during its continuance" (page 359); and further: "The action I took was in my discretion; in exercising his discretion, a minister must have regard to conditions, because conditions have a direct bearing upon the consequences attendant on his action to the bank and the general situation. If you make a mistake in putting in an auditor, in peace time the consequences may be a run producing little effect upon the bank; if in war time, you may bring down the bank and, in addition, you may cause an unspeakable calamity to the country." (page 743).
Your committee is not called upon to question the manner in which Sir Thomas White made use of the powers given to him, or whether he exercised his discretion correctly or otherwise.
Your committee consider that the facts brought out in the interim report submitted by Mr. Chief Justice McKeown, and the evidence therein referred to, establish that the depositors of the Home Bank have a moral claim in equity for compensation by the country on account of any loss they may suffer by reason of the failure of the Home Bank.
Thomas Vien,
Chairman.

Mr. W. G. RAYMOND (Brantford) presented the second and final report of the special committee appointed to make inquiry into an old age pension system for Canada, as follows:
Old Age Pensions

The Special Committee appointed to inquire into an old age pension system for Canada has the honour to present the following as its second and final report:
Your committee has inquired into the systems which are in operation in England, Australia, New Zealand and certain other countries, examined witnesses, carefully considered their suggestions, and compared the information obtained from thirty-one municipalities throughout Canada, in reply to a questionnaire sent to one hundred and thirty-five mayors of cities and towns in every province.
This question has been before this House at different times since 1907, but no definite recommendation was made by any of the committees to which it was referred.
After careful consideration of the information obtained from the sources enumerated, your committee respectfully recommends:
1.	That an old age pension system be established at the earliest possible date for deserving indigent persons to seventy (70) years of age and upwards.
2.	That applicants for pension must be British subjects of at least twenty (20) years' residence in Canada, or naturalized subjects of at least fifteen (15) years' naturalization and twenty-five (25) years' residence.
3.	(a) That the maximum rate of pension be twenty ($20) dollars per month which will be lessened by private income or partial ability to earn:
(b) That one-half the amount of pension payable be borne by the federal government; the other half, by the provincial governments of such provinces as express by legislation their desire to adopt the system -the cost of administration to be borne by the provincial governments.
Your committee has estimated that under such a system there would be approximately 98,841 eligible pensioners, and that if all of these were to receive the maximum rate of pension, namely, twenty ($20) dollars per month, the federal government's portion of the total yearly expenditure would amount to $11,860,920. This amount, however, would be reduced by any private income or partial earnings.
Your committee further recommends that the government communicate with the various provincial governments to ascertain if they are disposed to adopt the above system and enact the necessary legislation.
Your committee also begs to recommend that its proceedings together with the evidence taken, be printed as an appendix to the journals of this House.
For the information of the House, a copy of the proceedings and evidence, a synopsis of the communications received from the municipalities, and a statement of the expectation of life prepared by the Department of Insurance, are appended to this report.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
W. G. Raymond,
Chairman.
Is that a unanimous report .'rom the committee?
It is a unanimous report of the members present at the final meeting; all the members of the committee were not in attendance.

On the Orders of the Day:

Postal Employees

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct the attention of the government to the following fact, and to address to it the following inquiries in relation thereto:
Recently, at Victoria, B.C., Vice Admiral Sir Frederick Field, the principal speaker at a public luncheon given in honour of the British squadron visiting that city, is reported to have stated that he personally believed that Canada should equip and maintain four cruisers, two of which would be held on the Pacific and two on the Atlantic.
My first question is, whether the government invited this distinguished sailor to give this advice.
In the event of the answer to this question being in the negative, in view of the fact that this country is a loyal supporter of the League of Nations, is anxious to see naval and military expenditure cut to the minimum, is conscious that war has proved a dismal failure as a means of settling international disputes, is convinced that our financial solvency, if not our very civilization itself, depends on the reduction of armaments,-would the government take into consideration the advisability of communicating either directly with the gentleman in question, or through the appropriate officers of the state he serves, to the effect that such pronouncement as that delivered by the Vice Admiral on a matter of purely Canadian national policy is undesirable?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to
my hon. friend, I desire to say that the government did not invite Vice Admiral Field to make any such statement as is attributed to him. The well-recognized principle has always obtained that the question of how much shall be spent bj/ the Canadian people on naval or other services is a matter which rests with the Canadian government and parliament alone. In the past there have been occasions, I believe, when the government of the day has seen fit to invite opinions from the authorities in the Mother Country with respect to naval matters. On this occasion there has been no request for any such opinion or advice. Naturally the statement that is attributed to Vice Admiral Field is one which should not be considered merely upon the basis of a newspaper report, but I shall take steps to verify whether he uttered the statement in question, and then take whatever course may be deemed best in order to assert the well-recognized practice in regard to these matters.

Tell him to mind his
own business.

maintopic: LEAGUE OF NATIONS-LABOUR EMPLOYMENT OF CHILDREN AT SEA
speechtext: The object of this draft convention is merely to prohibit the employment of children under the age of fourteen years on vessels engaged in maritime navigation. The provincial school laws in Canada provide for the attendance of youths at school; the factory acts of the several provinces prohibit the employment of children under fourteen in industrial establishments; but there is no provision in the Canada Shipping Act which specifically forbids the employment of children under fourteen, and as it is doubtful if any youths under this age are employed on seagoing vessels from Canadian ports, it was thought that the proposal involved in the draft convention would be regarded as non-contentious. The draft convention has been ratified by Great Britain, Sweden, Roumania, Bulgaria and Esthonia. Ratification has been authorized by Denmark, Finland, Italy, Japan, Holland and Poland. Bills, and so forth, looking to ratification are pending in Spain, Belgium, Germany, Argentine, Chile, Cuba and Lithuania. Legislation has also been adopted on the subject in Norway and is in preparation in India.

Hon. JAMES MURDOCK (Minister of Labour) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to confirm a certain draft convention fixing the minimum age for the admission of young persons to employment as trimmers or stokers, adopted at Geneva on the 11th day of November, 1921, by a General Conference of the International Labour Organization of the League of Nations; to provide that any persons under the age of 18 years shall not be employed or work as trimmers or stokers on vessels engaged in maritime navigation excluding ships of war, vessels mainly propelled by other means than steam, and school ships or training ships.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Marcil in the chair.

I would like to ask the
minister if he would be willing to modify the resolution slightly so as to include ships of war as well as merchant ships.

I might be perfectly willing to do so but I do not think we could undertake to include that modification here. The draft convention which we are now undertaking to ratify did not take into consideration ships of war, and I fear that if that point was insisted upon the whole matter, so far as our ratification is concerned, would fall.
Canada was represented at the conference, of course?
Yes.

I see the point the minister brings out, but I do not see why those who are recommending this convention would object to our carrying out the principle underlying their recommendation a little further than they/ went themselves. I think they ought to be grateful to us.
I am not disagreeing with my hon. friend on that point.

Is there any valid reason why Canada should not take an independent position in this matter? We could agree with the convention as far as it goes and the general principle underlying it will oe embodied in the bill subsequently to be brought down; but speaking for Canada, and certainly we have that right, we could exempt Canadian children from serving on board ships of war.

My understanding is
that we would not be considered as ratifying the convention unless we ratified it in the specific terms in which it came to us from the International Labour Conference where it was adopted. On several questions, for instance on the eight-hour day, there has been a disposition on the part of some countries to adopt regulations varying somewhat from the convention that emanated from the first Washington Conference, and the result is that no action has been taken. So, if Canada is to be regarded as ratifying this convention as it came to us from the International Labour Conference of 1920, it has to be done in the specific terms in which it came to us as well as to other countries.

I think
I see a glint of sympathy in the eye of the Minister of Labour. I would therefore ask him to consider favourably the introduction of a bill, separate and distinct from the one in which we shall be ratifying this convention, which will set forth the ideas that I think we mutually have in mind.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF CHILDREN AT SEA-MEDICAL EXAMINATION

speechtext:
Hon. JAMES MURDOCK (Minister of Labour) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to confirm a certain Draft Convention concerning the Compulsory Medical Examinations of Children and Young Persons Employed at Sea, adopted at Geneva on the 11th day of November, 1921, by a General Conference of the International Labour Organization of the League of Nations; to provide that the employment of any child or young person under 18 years of age on any vessel engaged in maritime navigation, other than vessels on which only members of the same family are employed, shall be conditional on the production of a medical certificate attesting fitness for such work and that the continued employment at sea of children and young persons shall be conditional on the reipetition of medical examination at intervals of not more than one year.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

League of Nations-Labour

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF CHILDREN AT SEA-MEDICAL EXAMINATION
speechtext: I draw the minister's attention to the sentence "other than vessels on which only members of the same family are employed." maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF CHILDREN AT SEA-MEDICAL EXAMINATION
speechtext:

My understanding is that this exception is so as not to interfere with a family who are handling a sailing vessel, as a fishing boat, that might naturally be regarded as their home or regular place of residence. maintopic: EMPLOYMENT OF CHILDREN AT SEA-MEDICAL EXAMINATION
speechtext:
The convention is short
and, perhaps, if I read the document it will afford hon. members the information they want:
Draft Convention Concerning the Compulsory Medical Examination of Children and Young Persons Employed at Sea.
Article 1.-For the purpose of this convention, the term "vessel" includes all ships and boats, of any nature whatsoever, engaged in maritime navigation, whether publicly or privately owned; it excludes ships of war.
Article 2.-The employment of any child or young person under eighteen years of age on any vessel, other than vessels upon which only members of the same family are employed, shall be conditional on the production of a medical certificate attesting fitness for such work, signed by a doctor who shall be approved by the competent authority.
Article 3.-The continued employment at sea of any such child or young person shall be subject to the repetition of such medical examination at intervals of not more than one year, and the production, after each such examination, of a further medical certificate
attesting fitness for such work. Should medical certificate expire in the course of the voyage it shall remain in force until the end of said voyage.
Article 4. In urgent cases, the competent authority may allow a young person below the age of eighteen years to embark without having undergone the examination provided for in Articles 2 and 3 of this convention, always provided that such an examination shall be undergone at the first port at which the vessel calls.
Article 5. Each member of the international labour organization which ratifies this convention engages to apply it to its colonies, possessions and protectorates, in accordance with the provisions of articles 421 of the Treaty of Versailles and of the corresponding articles of the other treaties of peace.

Hon. JAMES MURDOCK (Minister of Labour) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to confirm a certain draft convention concerning unemployment indemnity in case of loss or foundering of the ship, adopted at Genoa on the 9th day of July, 1920, by a general conference of the International labour organization of the League of Nations; and to provide that in the case of loss or foundering of any vessel the service of a seaman shall terminate before the date contemplated in the agreement, he shall be paid unemployment indemnity for the days during which he remains in fact unemployed for a period not exceeding two months.
Motion agreed to, and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

This convention is very short, and if I read it, possibly its meaning will be clear to hon. members. It reads:
Draft Convention Concerning Unemployment Indemnity in Case of Loss or Foundering of a Ship Article 1. For the purpose of this convention the term " seamen " includes all persons employed on any vessel engaged in maritime navigation. For the purpose of this convention the term " vessel " includes all ships and boats of any nature whatsoever, engaged in maritime navigation, whether publicly or privately owned; it excludes ships of war.
Article 2. In every case of loss or foundering of any vessel, the owner or person with whom the seaman has contracted for service on board the vessel shall pay to each seaman employed thereon an indemnity against unemployment resulting from such loss or foundering.
This indemnity shall be paid for the days during which the seaman remains in fact unemployed at the same rate as the wages payable under the contract, but the total indemnity payable under this convention to any one seaman may be limited to two months' wages.
Article 3. Seamen shall have the same remedies for recovering such indemnities as they have for recovering arrears of wages earned during the service.
Article 4. Each member of the International Labour Organization which ratifies this convention engages to apply it to its colonies, protectorates and possessions which are not fully self-governing:
(a)	Except where owing to the local conditions its provisions are inapplicable; or
(b)	Subject to such modifications as may be necessary to adopt its provisions to local conditions.
Each member shall notify to the International Labour Office the action taken in respect of each of its colonies, protectorates and possessions which are not fully self-governing.

There is a technical
point in connection with this resolution. 
Should not the word "if" be inserted in the fifth line? It says:
It is expedient to bring in a measure to confirm a certain draft convention concerning unemployment indemnity in case of loss or foundering of the ship, adopted at Genoa on the 9th day of July, 1920, by a general conference of the international labour organization of the League of Nations; and to provide that in the case of loss or foundering of any vessel the service of a seaman shall terminate before the date contemplated in the agreement, he shall be paid unemployment indemnity.
I think it should read: "if in the case of loss", and so on.
It will not hurt at all, but I really do not think it is necessary.

I do not know what it
means. It provides that:
In tJho case of loss or foundering of any vessel the service of a seaman shall terminate before the date contemplated.
Why should we provide that the service shall terminate? If we pass the resolution as it is we are providing that the service shall terminate, and we do not want to do that. We want ito provide that if the service terminates at such a time then the men shall be paid.

I think my right hon.
friend is right.

It is clear that this is
intended merely to impose an obligation on the vessel owner; that is to say, in his contract he must provide for certain payments to be made to the (men not only for any days they may be unemployed during the term of the contract but for a maximum of two months extra in the case of the foundering of the vessel.
Yes, that is right.
Amendment agreed to.

One of the objections I intended to raise has already been stated by the leader of the apposition. I have another reason for objecting ito the resolution however; it seems to me that every provision is being made for the seamen and none whatever for the person who may sustain considerable loss through the foundering of his vessel. The vessel owner might lose his ship and be ruined, yet he becomes responsible for two months' wages to the seamen on board who survive the disaster, even although he may be utterly unable to pay them. There is too little consideration on the one hand and too much on the other.

Is it not reasonable
to assume that the vessel will be insured?

League of Nations-Labour

Let us assume also
that in some cases vessels may not be insured. In any such case is the vessel owner to be responsible for the maintenance of the men for two months?

We are entitled to
take it for granted that every vessel owner will follow the usual practice and have his vessel insured.

How many nations have
adopted similar legislation?

So far the convention
has been ratified only by Bulgaria and Esthonia. Ratification has been authorized by Great Britain, Italy, Holland and Poland. The necessary procedure has been set in motion for ratification in Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Spain, Lithuania, Cuba, the Argentine Republic and Chile. Legislation on the subject has also been introduced in Norway.

Apparently, then, this legislation, in the course of four years, although contemplated by all these countries, has been adopted only by two small nations. What is the attitude of the United States to a regulation of this kind, which might seriously add to the cost of shipping?

The United States is not a member of the League of Nations and therefore does not hold membership in the international labour organization. I think however that its shipping laws in respect of the matters covered in these resolutions are about on the same basis as the legislation we now propose. One of the reasons why this matter has not been pressed before is Canada's reluctance to precede Great Britain in regard to such questions. I believe that only in one of the four instances we have under consideration this afternoon has Great Britain actually ratified the legislation, but in the other cases, as in this, ratification has been authorized. Of course, it will be some time before we reach the point of ratification even although these resolutions become effective in the shape of bills; there is a certain necessary form of procedure for the purpose and it has not been thought proper to try to get ahead of the Mother Country in ratifying these conventions.

My hon. friend
opposite (Mr. McMaster) assumes that all vessels would be insured, but there are a great many small boats on the lakes and elsewhere which, I can quite understand, might not be insured at all. In some cases the insurance might lapse through some oversight,
or the owner might not be in a position to get insurance. Are we to make that owner responsible for two months' wages for the survivors of a wreck notwithstanding an entire loss on his own part? Surely the men might be expected to find employment in some other capacity within a short time after the loss of the vessel. I do not think that the fact that Bulgaria and Esthonia, two small nations, have so far adopted similar legislation is sufficient warranty for this parliament passing this law at the present time. I think we could very well allow the matter to stand for a while and see whether the other nations are going to pass this legislation. As to this resolution becoming effective when the bill is adopted by this House, it certainly will go into force when the act is signed by the Governor General, and we shall be linked up then with Bulgaria and Esthonia as three countries forming the advance guard in this matter. This legislation pays absolutely no regard to the vessel owner who might lose everything, but it makes him responsible for the maintenance of his crew after the foundering of his ship. It does not seem to be at all pressing, and in view of the stated desire of the government to get through with the work of the session as soon as possible I do not think that any serious hardship will ensue if the matter is deferred for another year, or not passed at all.

It is not often that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sutherland) and I agree, but I am in sympathy with the statement he has'made; this legislation is not called for. I can remember an incident that occurred on the Pacific coast a little over a year ago. A widow owned a steamer which was not insured and which was lost; and that steamer was all that she had. Why should the crew be enabled to sue her for wages for two months while they go about idle? I repeat, the legislation is entirely uncalled for. Thirty days is about the limit of compensation a man can claim who is dismissed in ordinary occupations, why give seamen sixty days? Are they going to be a privileged class of people in this country?
Mr. MURDO'OK:	My hon. friend must
remember that two months is not the minimum but the maximum.

The minister may rest
assured that the maximum will be claimed every time.

Let us take the case suggested by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Stuherland), of a vessel foundering on any of the lakes. Is it reasonable to
League of Nations-Labour

suppose that a seaman in that case could claim wages for sixty days? That seems to me to be far-fetched, because that man could easily get around to his home in a couple of days. Sixty days is the maximum and it is intended to apply in the case of seamen who are shipwrecked at a considerable distance from home, perhaps a thousand miles or so; the provision is that such a man should be paid two months' wages to enable him to return home if he is unemployed.

I do not think the
committee need feel that sailors are going to be a privileged class. They are away from home most of the time, they are not present to urge their claims upon members of parliament and other public men, and therefore I think it behooves legislators to look after their interests. It seems to me that this is a very reasonable provision. The case cited by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) is, I think, a very extreme one, as the Minister of Labour has pointed out. The object of the convention seems very clear and plain. Sailors may be wrecked some distance from home before their agreement is up, and in that case the steamship owner, who as a rule will be insured, will be responsible for the unemployment indemnity, not exceeding two months. It is true, as pointed out by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride), that there may be such a case as he brought before the House, of a widow woman, a ship owner, whose ship was lost and was not insured. But I think that will be found to be the exception, for it is one of the primary canons of the shipping business to have vessels insured. It is only the very largest steamship lines that carry their own insurance. I think it will be found that a very large proportion of the world's shipping is insured, as it should be. Insurance facilities are such that every reasonably practical vessel owner will have his ship insured against this contingent liability. This convention has been arrived at after careful consideration by all interested parties, and it behooves us to follow it. The argument has been brought forward that only two small nations have actually ratified the legislation. Well, the leader of the Conservative party (Mr. Meighen) stated in the House fhe other day that "Canada should lead the way." I forget exactly in what connection he made that statement, but it expresses an excellent sentiment-a sentiment that should appeal to all of us on Dominion Day.

I used the expression in relation to the attitude of the dominions in Empire affairs, that Canada being first and

largest should lead. I do not take broad exception to the views expressed by the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), but I really have not the same conception of the meaning of the clause that the Minister of Labour has, if I understood him rightly. He emphasized the fact that this is the maximun.

Not exceeding two
months.

Yes. But the effect is
this, that the sailor every time, providing his own master cannot take him on again within the period before the two months expire, can always claim the whole two months' 'indemnity. I think the member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) is right in that respect.
It is not likely that the sailor will be so unfortunate as to be subject to constant founderings of his ship.

The member has missed
the point. The maximum has this effect in all cases of foundering, that unless the master of the ship can get his vessel back into service again before the two months expire, he would be compelled to pay right to the limit of the two months.

Unless the sailor found
employment elsewhere.

The sailor has no incentive to find employment elsewhere when he is paid up to the full two months anyway. That is really what is in the minds of the member for Cariboo and the member for South Oxford.

It seems to me that
this will happen-either he will be wrecked near his home, where it is to be presumed he will be able to find employment again; or if he is wrecked away from home it will be natural for him to take service in the ship that first presents itself giving him reasonably attractive opportunities of service. I think the objections raised to this convention are not serious; there is of course something to be said on the other side, but it seems to me that the object of the legislation will appeal to everybody, namely, not to allow a sailor who has been wrecked some distance from home to be stranded without some resource that he can call upon.

This convention was
adopted at the International Labour Conference of 1920 without a dissenting voice from the representatives of any nation, from any of the employers' representatives, from any of the employees' representatives, Mr. Thomas

League of Nations-Labour
Robb, manager of the Shipping Federation of Canada, was the employers' representative at that conference, he also agreed to the convention.
That being the case, how is it that only those two small nations have ratified?

For the same reason, I think, that we have not ratified it, there is nothing so very pressing and urgent as to necessitate its immediate ratification. But when we are in the position of giving effect to some of the conventions that emanated from the International Labour Conference, it appeared to be reasonable to couple up these four resolutions so as to incorporate them in the Canada Shipping Act at one and the same time. Practically the conditions proposed are in effect now, except this one, and I have not heard any complaint in this respect. But it is merely a question of proceeding not too hurriedly but in an orderly way to give effect to some of these conventions, if we can, because my hon. friend from South Oxford knows that at times questions are asked, such as: Why has Canada not given effect to some of the conventions emanating from the International Labour Conference? We are trying to do so on matters that are not seriously handicapping to Canada and are not of very serious moment to Canadians, but which will show that we are at least ready to take a step in the right direction.
Would this act apply to coastwise shipping or only to ocean-going vessels?

My understanding is that should this be incorporated in the Canada Shipping Act it would apply only to such vessels as come within the provisions of that act. I am of opinion that the widow's vessel which my hon. friend referred to a short time ago would not be covered by this convention because it would not be of sufficient tonnage.
But I want to know definitely whether this applies to coastwise shipping or only to ocean-going vessels.

I would suggest that it
ought to apply to coastwise shipping.
It applies to all shipping that is covered by the Canada Shipping Act.

I should think the question was covered by the former answer of the Minister of Labour, that he thought the convention covered lake shipping. If that be the case, it is perfectly obvious that coastal shipping is also covered by this convention.

No doubt the Canada Shipping Act does apply to coastwise shipping. But in that case the principal complaint of the hon. member for South Oxford will disappear because men on coastal boats-and I presume on lake boats also-are paid by the month. Therefore in the event of their ship being wrecked they would get a month's notice, and consequently their unemployment payment would not extend beyond that period, because the resolution provides:
That if in the case of loss or foundering of any vessel the service of a seaman shall terminate before the date contemplated in the agreement.
The owner of the coastwise vessel would therefore be liable only for a month's indemnity.

I am inclined to
think, if that is the case, that even though the seamen were employed monthly they would be entitled to two months' indemnity. The Minister of Labour himself admits that inside of two days a sailor on the Great Lakes ought to be able to obtain other employment. I cannot see the wisdom of providing two months' holidays for any one who sees fit to take advantage of this legislation. If the bill goes into effect, as stated by the hon. member (Mr. McBride) it wall enable men employed monthly to draw two months' salary after a wreck takes place.

I suppose they will get
wrecked regularly in order to get some easy money.

I can imagine the
hon. member for Brome as the advance agent for the insurance companies when he points out that the large steamship companies carry their own insurance.
I said only the largest, and I think I am right.

Only the largest
carry their own insurance. Well, if the large owners can carry their own insurance surely the same thing should not be denied the smaller owners.

The large companies
have enough ships to ensure that the law of average shall apply, and they can carry their own risks, and sometimes do with safety. The small owner who owns only one or two ships cannot afford to run the risk, so he has to pay an insurance premium to cover the risk. I submit that the legislation sought is highly proper and highly desirable. Surely no one in this House wishes to deprive a sailor who is wrecked of a chance of being protected in his livelihood for a maximum
League oj Nations-Labour

of sixty days. If some vessel owners do not insure their vessels, this is an added reason why they should. If it induces them to insure where otherwise they would not, then we are conferring a benefit, not imposing a hardship upon them.

The inference seems
to be that the vessel owner who is insured loses nothing if he loses his vessel. It is well known, however, that you cannot insure a building or a vessel or anything else on the basis of its full value, so that in addition to the amount paid in premiums, which has to be added to overhead, the owner is possibly out the equivalent of one-third the cost of his vessel. I cannot help agreeing with the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) and the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) that the time is too long. As I understand it, even if a man is employed by the month, if his employment ceases before the end of the month he can still claim two months' pay.

I think he can, if he is actually out of work. The sailor as a rule is not the most provident of men; he has not made savings; and he is doing some of the most hazardous and necessary work of the world, exposing his health and very life in the service of humanity. Surely he is entitled to get sixty days' unemployment insurance at the expense of the owner if he is out of a job for that length of time. I think we are balking over something which really ought to appeal to all of us.

All I can say is that the
hon. member (Mr. McMaster) does not know what he is talking about. If he was in the shipping business for some time he would think differently. I have had a good deal to do with sailors. I have been a sailor myself, and I say that the sailor often has a mighty good time when out at sea, much easier than he would have if he were working on a farm.
I think the period should be cut down to thirty days.

Can we not deal with
this matter when the bill is taken up?
I have no doubt that if the hon. member (Mr. McMaster) were a ship owner he would not say what he has just said.
Now, why impute such unworthy motives?

I am agreeing with what
my hon. friend has just said.

There is no reason to
be wrong just in order to be polite.

I am not sure I am wrong
in coming to that conclusion, because naturally in that position my hon. friend would be looking after his own personal interests. But a ship may be wrecked through the carelessness of the owner, who may not have attended to the vessel or kept it in proper condition. Further, when the sailor is wrecked he may lose all his clothing, all his belongings, in fact, and be set ashore with nothing but what he is walking in. I think that the resolution ought to pass without further discussion.

The minister has
pointed out that this legislation is not urgent. In view of the fact that we are in the month of July and that the session will in all probability run for a considerable time yet I must protest against the introduction of legislation at this time that is not urgent. Not only that, but it is another form of this nursing legislation that we are continually passing, making people do something that the government should not interfere in at all. We are continually passing restrictions and regulations, a little here and a little there as to how people shall carry on their business,-* in other words, putting a premium on laziness and inefficiency and a penalty on enterprise and energy.

Is the hon. member
referring to protection or to this bill?

Only the other day a measure was introduced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) to enable lawyers to charge about three times what they had been charging for entering notices of protest. These are some of the things that tend to bring law into contempt, in this country. The hon. member (Mr. McMaster) has referred to our passing legislation of this kind on Dominion Day. It is an unjustifiable offence that this parliament should be in session on our great national holiday, when we ought to be doing something towards the development of a national spirit in our people instead of dealing with trifling legislation of this kind for which the minister says there is not the least urgency. So far only two countries, Bulgaria and Esthonia, have passed legislation in accordance with the draft convention of the 1920 conference. That was four years ago. Yet on Dominion Day this House must sit to deal with a trifling resolutions of this kind to suit the Minister of Labour.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Murdock thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 216,

Refunding Loan
to amend the Canada Shipping Act to give effect to certain draft conventions adopted by the International Labour Conference of the League of Nations.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakeroldname: Eight Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill
which has just received its first reading includes, I understand, all the provisions based on the first two resolutions we have passed. Bills were introduced by error with respect to the first two resolutions, and I therefore move, seconded by Mr. Murdock:
That the first readings of Bills Nos. 214 and 215 based on the resolutions adopted in committee of the Whole this day and standing as Nos. 31 and 37 of the Orders of the Day be rescinded.
Motion agreed to.

Hon. J. A. ROBB (Acting Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide authority for the raising, by way of loan, under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, by the issue and sale or pledge of securities of Canada, in such form, for such separate sums, at such rate of interest and upon such other terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may approve, such sum or sums of money as may be required, but not to exceed in the whole the sum of three hundred million dollars, for paying maturing loans and obligations of Canada, and to provide that the principal so raised by way of loan and the interest thereon shall be a charge upon and payable out of the consolidated revenue fund.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, this is the usual
method when the government requires authority to take care of maturing obligations or to provide for new obligations. This is entirely to take care of maturing obligations up to and including 1927. The situation is this. On 1st November, 1924, we have $107,955,650 of the 1919 victory loan falling due. In 1922, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) introduced a bill which was passed, authorizing the raising of loans up to $350,000,000 for refunding purposes. The renewal loan of 1922 was for $114,464,150. The refunding loan of 1923 was for $200,000,000. This leaves a borrowing power from the 1922 bill still available of $35,535,850. The purpose of this bill is to provide borrowing powers in the future for maturing loans and obligations.
I will give hon. gentlemen the maturing loans and obligations for the next three years.
On 1st November, 1924, there is due a victory loan of $107,955,650; and in October and November, 1924, outstanding treasury bills going back to the war date amounting to $4,680,000; §41,060,000; $19,325,000; $26,250,000.
When were those issued?

They are treasury bills issued
during the war period. They have been renewed from time to time, as my hon. friend will recall. Then, on May 1, 1925, we have a bond issue due in London of $24,333,333.33.
What is the total of the treasury bills?

Calculating it at the moment, they amount to over $91,000,000. In 1925 there is maturing on 1st May, $24,333,333.33; on 1st July, $60,800; and on 1st December, -this is the war loan of 1915-$42,014,500. In 1926 we have maturing on 1st April, $25,000,000; on 1st November, 1927, $29,068,400; and on 1st December, $63,437,250. The total is $382,184,933.33. We are asking for authority in this resolution to take care of these maturing obligations.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

What official of
the government keeps a record of the public debt, and what sort of ledger is it kept in?
I would like to have a little information about that, having in view that the time may soon arrive when we could have a better consolidation of our public debt, and on a broader plan than has been pursued in the past.

The Chief Accountant is Mr. Macfarlane, in the Department of Finance. That is all under the administration of the Deputy Minister of Finance. I quite agree with my hon. friend that we should look forward to the time wThen the interest rate may become so favourable that we might consolidate our debt obligations.

Have you that
always in view? Hitherto it seems-I know very little about it-that a rather slipshod practice has been followed. There ought to be a broad policy in dealing with the national debt. There ought to be a ledger showing the national debt and the due dates. I do not believe any member of this House ever saw that ledger; I do not know whether there is one or not; I do not know whether anybody has ever seen the diary in which these due dates are entered. Somehow I have the impression that there ought to be a better
Refunding Loan

organization for dealing with this question, and it may come up in this House this week. The time will come when there should be a reorganization of the Finance department with a responsible officer at the head, with the present branches of the department consolidated under one high official of the government, say a Comptroller of the Currency, or an officer of that kind.

Where does the minister
intend to float this loan?
In the best market available.

The minister should not answer the question that way. What is in his mind as to the best policy, whether to endeavour to float in Canada or out of Canada; and if out of Canada, whether in England or the United States? The main question, though, of interest for hon. members is whether the minister really contemplates a domestic loan or not.
I propose to get the money wherever it can be procured to the best advantage of the taxpayers of Canada.
What is the minister's idea?

We will have to look into
that. There will be lots of time between now and November to study the condition of the money market.
I do not think it is a matter of the market at all; it is a matter of policy. There are different opinions as to the wisdom of floating a loan in Canada or in other countries.
I should like to have my right hon. friend's views right now. I am looking for advice on the subject.

Your right hon. friend does not pretend to be much of a financier. His opportunities of learning from this government in that respect have not been very great; but I am sure we will be enlightened by the minister's experience in the last year. What is the minister's view on the subject?

I have just given my views. Now I am looking for advice. I agree with my right hon. friend. There are people who come to you and say you should float this loan in Canada; and there are others who say you should get more new money into the country. I have not been able to make up my mind on the subject.

My suggestion is that the Acting Minister of Finance should take up in a broad way the question of the public debt of Canada-that is to consolidate the debt and perhaps get money at a lower rate of interest than has been possible in the last thirty years. To-day in New York money is at a lower rate than it has been for many years, and if we approach the question in the broad way I have indicated the results may be most advantageous to Canada. If this question is discussed as it should be the minister may get valuable suggestions even from hon. members on this side; the subject is worthy of adequate discussion and the getting of full information in regard to it. It would certainly appear to be the proper time to consolidate the public debt when the rate of interest in New York is as low as it is to-day. Let us take a broad view of the question and see if we cannot save some of the money we now pay in our annual interest charges.

I do not see why the minister does not welcome expressions of opinion as to whether this loan should be floated in Canada or in some other country. My own opinion is that we have floated too many loans in this country; and if we now place another loan of three hundred millions in Canada it will tie up money that would serve to keep the wheels of industry rolling. There is too much money locked up as it is, and people are finding it hard to collect their accounts. If the minister insists on raising this loan in Canada there will be no money available for commercial or industrial purposes. If you go to a bank to-day you cannot get money; you are told it is all tied up in victory bonds or other war loans, and if you are now going to float another three hundred million loan you are only going to aggravate the situation.
Oh, no.
That is the intention, I understand.
That is a misunderstanding. This is to take care of bonds that are now outstanding, of loans that were floated in Canada by the government which my hon. friend supported.

I am opposed to such a policy. I do not see how you are going to raise such a loan and pay 5 or 5i per cent.
I understand that money is available in New York at 3 or 3J per cent. It is much better to get the money there than to raise a loan in this country.

I cannot raise a loan anywhere until this bill goes through.

Refunding Loan
The minister ought to be frank enough to give the committee some information as to what he is going to do in this matter.
Perhaps my hon. friend was out when I made the statement a few moments ago that I am going to raise the money in the best market available.

Is the minister going to get the money in the cheapest market-that is taking into account the cost of commissions and so forth-or is he going to raise the loan irrespective of general economic considerations?

The question raised by the right hon. leader of the opposition and the hon. memiber for Parkdale is a very important question indeed, one which I think is sometimes lost sight of in general policies of government. In the past we have been frequently told that the raising of money by way of a loan in Canada is the best thing to do. We have also 'been told on many an occasion that owning our own debt is a very excellent thing for the people of this country.
I must say that I have not particularly shared that view at all. Mr. Chairman, I would answer an observation made by the hon. member for Mackenzie. He states that whenever under the Finance Act the banks take securities and deposit them with the government there is inflation. I do not agree with that statement. Inflation is where you increase either the actual money or the bank credit of the country beyond the actual needs of the country. An increase in credit, whether it is in the form of dollar bills or in bank credit, which merely keeps pace with the increase of the business of the country is not inflation. One of the factors which tend to prevent inflation under the Finance Act is that banks are obliged when they borrow money on the securities which they deposit with the government to pay the interest upon them. It is true they borrow the money for the purpose of lending it again at a profit, but they have always got the interest to pay; and then of course they have the solvency and the soundness of their institution to bear in mind-considerations which should operate to prevent them from making undue use of this advantage.

With any system that

You will find no infallible rule in any system of banking or of credit; mistakes will be made. But the value of such a discussion as this-and I am doubtful whether this is the proper time and place for it-is to attract public attention to what are the real bases of the credit of the country. We have been too much accustomed to regard money as consisting in the mere dollar bills or ten or twenty dollar bills which happen to be in the pockets or the tills of the people. But I think I am right in stating that not more than 10 per cent of the business transactions of the country are conducted with currency; 90 per cent are conducted through the credit system which really comes down to nothing more nor less than entries in the books of the bankers of the country. What I wanted to point out when I rose in the first place was that for bankers to take sound securities to the government and in exchange for them to get currency which can be used in the business of the country is not of necessity inflation. If it is for the purpose and is limited to the object of creating enough credit instruments to keep pace with but not to run ahead of the business of the country it is not necessarily inflation.

Since you have ruled

Take, for instance, a farmer in good circumstances. He has horses and cattle, farm implements, grain and land. He is known to be a reliable man who meets his obligations. He issues a note, say, for $100. Anybody who has money to lend would take that note if it had a reasonable time to run. But suppose he issues a similar note every day in the week for months, or every hour in the day-why, the notes would very soon be far below par; a little later they would be worth very little, and finally they would be worth nothing at all. A nation could do the same thing by issuing its paper to excess. We have seen Russia, Austria and Germany do it until their paper became worthless.

Has any one in this
House to-day suggested issuing paper to excess?

I am not stating that, but I think that is implied in the arguments of some hon. gentlemen on the other side. The government of Canada issues paper currency; the banks of Canada issue paper currency, and between the two issues the full requirements of the people are met. If the government decided upon issuing a much larger quantity of this paper than is now in circulation there would be no room for it unless the privileges and the powers the banks have in respect to the issuing of currency were taken away, and that would raise a very big [Mr. Robb.l
question. If those privileges and powers were taken away the government could issue its own paper without inflating the currency, without reaching the danger point. At some seasons of the year more currency is required than at other seasons, and the government would have to be in a position to take care of the excess currency as it was presented by giving for it something that would have an international value-for instance, gold. The government evidently could not redeem its own excess issue by another issue. That is the full limit to which the government could go. In my judgment the government could not issue any more notes than are now in circulation, because the people of Canada could not absorb them; they are not needed in the daily business of the country, and could no-t therefore be issued unless the government withdrew from the banks the power and privilege they now possess. a direct ratio between commodities and currency. Of course there are other matters of inflation and they are somewhat connected with the subject I have just alluded to. Take for example government bonds. One of the greatest causes of inflation in every country was the issue of government bonds, and the re-issue of them and the use in different re-issues of practically the original dollar with some enlargement of the principal. That alone of itself does not make inflation. Hon. gentlemen talk about loans being made by banks to customers, and treat that fact as if it creates inflation. It does not so long as it is proper business. Supposing, for example, that those government loans had been for the purpose of enlarging our agricultural and industrial activities, costing 5 to 6 per cent but bringing in as a result i f the enlargement of those activities a return of 10 per cent? There is no inflation there. On the contrary, instead of inflation you have a very useful investment. But these government loans were not for any of these useful things. Why, there was not one victory loan that had anything really useful lor its purpose except enabling business to be carried on for the time. seas. Everything was being blown up, our money was being dissipated, and therefore there was inflation.

In the first instance hon, gentlemen are not quite right when they think that all of the bonds of this country are held or very largely or almost exclusively held by the big corporations. On the other hand, if they cannot use it, if you have a great deal of money that cannot be used and if it is not redeemable, then of course you have the Russian or German situation. It could not be redeemable. Just follow up the thought that is thrown out. We pay these obligations by issuing paper. That paper cannot be redeemed.

I have made no
suggestion of issuing paper. I simply asked whether the credit was not the same whether the government borrowed through the banks or re-issued creditory notes or bills. The credit is the same in .either case, I think, and there would be no more inflation in the one case than in the other.

Suppose you
take this view of it; suppose we do not use the banks or the underwriters at all, and do just what we did in the case of the victory loans, it is quite all right. In reference to that loan we looked after our own business. We made our own agreement and did our own advertising. We negotiated with ino underwriters. We raised the money ourselves. I did not know this matter was coming up; I am speaking from memory, and hon. members will bear with me if my figures are not quite accurate, but they are substantially correct, and I say that the victory loans cost us 0.7, 0.9, 1.3, and 1.1, if I remember rightly. We did all the work ourselves. The department itself looked after it, but hon. gentlemen will see what that meant. That meant absolutely no change in the underlying principle. What is that principle? The principle is that the country as a country gives the security which is a redeemable security, and it makes no difference whether the security is a bond, a bill or a lien, so long as we have to redeem it, and if we issue bonds to-day and say to these gentlemen, "Here we will give you bonds, -whether you want them or not, or we will give you a legal, whether you want it or not"; we are not paying them, and we can very well say that that is something that is going to be redeemable when we are treating these existing obligations as not redeemable. This is a matter in which we want all the
Refunding Loan

light we can get. I am afraid at present the only practical method is to do business either ourselves directly upon the recognized basis of values, or else deal through the banks.

I wish to make a suggestion in all seriousness to the minister, and I deal with this subject in no flippant or purely academic fashion. I look upon this matter as one of the most serious problems facing not only Canada but other nations. I say that this government, in common with other governments, are absolutely in the power of financial interests at the present_moment, and are unable-to-frec-them..-selves from the shackles of those interests.
I have before me statements from prominent gentlemen in regard to this matter. I have under my hand a statement from the Prime Minister of England, Ramsay MacDonald, in which he declares that all governments were helpless in the power of the financial classes.
I have Lord Milner's similar statement in that connection, and a further quotation that deals directly with this particular problem. He says: .
As a matter of fact some of the greatest fortunes have been made and are being made to-day by the mere manipulation of financial counters for which the chaos of exchange affords such exceptional opportunity. That is interception in the grand style.
By giving the minister permission to float this loan of 3300.000,000 we are proposing, I understand, that the minister shall forthwith adopt the orthodox practice of issuing bonds through the regular orthodox channels. In short, we are continuing the practice of the past, in still recognizing the financial machine that exists and are using that machine without always taking into consideration just what it means in cost to the people. If the minister has to float three hundred million dollars' worth of thirty-year bonds at five per cent interest, what does it involve? This is a consideration that should be thoroughly impressed on the public and also on the minister.
It means that if the bonds run to maturity we in Canada and our children after us-because we will not all live thirty years longer -will have paid four hundred and fifty millions in interest for the use of about two hundred and ninety-two million, and we would still owe the three hundred million to the bondholders whoever they may be. I term that frankly a most insane system of financing in this age and generation. I therefore urge the minister to take into consideration some alternative method, not with a view to immediately adopting it-I do not attempt to suggest I could induce him to do that.,-but I ask him and the ministers that may follow him

in his department, to take into consideration this appalling cumulative debt that is pressing upon the backs of nations to-day, 265 billions of international debts, the result largely of cumulative interest on bonds. Wheie is it going to stop? How will we pay it? The industrial machine is cracking to the breaking point at this moment. That is the situation.
Mr. \ IEN:	Has the hon. member any
alternative to suggest?

We have
suggested one very carefully this afternoon, -and-that-is-that-the-government might Aake-into consideration the possibility of accepting its own real credit, a real credit which J. P. Morgan will accept, and issue thereupon judiciously and wisely its own financial credit.

Would the minister not consider the question of appointing a permanent committee to study the national debt? Probably they could extend the powers of the committee on Banking and Commerce, and have it reconstructed as the committee on Public Debt and Banking. Every session that committee could review the public debt, as to its location and the interest to be paid on it, and propound a scheme for the refunding of it. If that were done, the result would be that gradually an active and an informed committee in connection with public debt would be developed in this House, and that committee would accomplish some of the things that this House now as a committee is trying to do to-night. I have never known of any real parliamentary study by this House of the public debt in relation to the rate of interest and consolidation later on. Perhaps the minister will make a statement in regard to the suggestion which has come not ;only from myself but from several hon. gentlemen who have spoken to-day.

The suggestion that has come from the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) has I think very considerable merit. It is a singular and very significant fact that, connected with a number of our departments of government, particularly the Department of Agriculture, we have some really expert and well qualified men to guide us. And while I wish to say nothing disparaging about the estimable gentlemen who are associated with the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), I think I state only the bald truth when I say there is no one in that department who is in any sense qualified to advise the minister in matters of this sort.
