(Mr. MARLER: Why does the hon. member say that? Does he mean to impugn the ability of the officers of the Department of Finance?
The hon. member (Mr. Good) is referring to their knowledge of financial affairs.
The officers of the Department of Finance are in my opinion an exceedingly able and intelligent lot of men.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I desire to remind hon. gentlemen that the present trend of the debate is out of order; this is not a question of appointing a committee.
Mr. 'GOOD: Perhaps the discussion from that standpoint is out of order, and I do not know whether I am permitted to answer the question put to me by the hon. gentleman.
I am expressing my opinion however, not without due consideration and considerable inquiry from people who are much more competent to form an opinion than I am myself. It is high time that, associated with the Minister of Finance and his deputy, there should be one or more persons who have extensive training in this particular branch, training altogether different from the kind which the present Deputy Minister of Finance has had.

The people the hon. gentleman has in mind are no better judges than some others.
Mr. 'GOOD: I have expressed my opinion; let it stand for what it is worth.
It is not worth very much.

I want to refer particularly to a criticism offered by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) of what he supposed was a suggestion emanating from this quarter of the House as to the payment of our debts and the settlement of the $300,000,000. The ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) referred to the same matter. The question is asked:	"Why do we not issue our own
promises to pay or Dominion notes for the amount of the debt and wipe it out that way?" And that suggestion is ridiculed. I admit that generally speaking such a practice is a very foolish one, but there might be conditions under which it oould be carried on not only with impunity but with profit. I discussed this matter last year with Professor Irving Fisher, one who, probably, has made a closer study of it than any other person on the American continent. I asked him particularly as to the propriety of such a practice, because I could see very serious disadvantages in it, as no doubt everyone else can; and he said that the advantage of it depended wholly on conditions. I do not wish to go into the matter any further than to say that while the practice is not always a wise one, there are nevertheless certain conditions under which it might profitably be indulged in under proper regulations.

Did he define the conditions?
Mr. 'GOOD: Yes, but that is a matter which I shall deal with in another debate.
What practical knowledge had he of the situation? Had he any practical interest?
I believe so, yes. At any rate, I quote the opinion as that of a man of authority who has studied the question.
Theoretically.

There is only one other matter I want to deal with in this connection. If we were to present to any of our bankers what is admittedly a questionable method of financing, they would hold up their hands in horror.
Because they know their business.

They would say, "Let us do it in the regular, orthodox and proper way". I want hon. members to figure out how the banker does it in the orthodox and proper way. Here is a loan of $300,000,000. How much of that will be inflation?-if we use that term, as it has been used, perhaps improperly. How much of it will be new money and how much the absorption of purchasing power already in existence? Let me suggest what the banker might do-and I submit that he often actually does it; it was done during the war time and time again as can be proved. He may take $100,000,000 of that sum out of existing purchasing power and put $200,000,000 of new money with it, and the country will not see the $200,000,000 of new money because the other is put up in front of it, as was said last year, as a smoke screen; and that will be done not necessarily deliberately but perhaps unconsciously. Here is the very practice we object to, and rightly, in the printing of paper money without limit or regulation; and yet we allow our bankers a free hand in this matter, to inflate or deflate credit without regulation. That is the trouble and that is what may happen.
In conclusion, I would again urge upon the Acting Minister of Finance that he seek
Refunding Loan

expert advice in this matter and consider the situation very carefully before he launches out this fall on a programme of floating loans. And I would emphasize once more the importance of his obtaining competent outside advice. In saying this I wish to cast no reflection whatever upon the personal character, the integrity or the faithfulness of those who are associated with the minister; but I am satisfied, and I say it in the kindliest spirit, that his deputy is quite incompetent to advise him in a matter of this nature.

First of all, let me say in reply to my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) that there is no question affecting our Canadian life that deserves so much attention as the consideration, when the time is opportune, of the question of consolidating the public debt and reducing if we can the interest we have to pay. I will keep the hon. gentleman's observations in mind. As to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Good), I want to disclaim any pretensions to the expert knowledge of a financier; as hon. gentlemen know, I am carrying on the work of this office in the temporary absence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) whose illness we all regret. However, in justice to the Deputy Minister of Finance I must say that I have never found any more loyal or willing public servant than the gentleman who serves this country in that capacity. He has been in the service of Canada since he was a boy.
I did not say otherwise.

He has grown up in it and is conversant with all its details. He is a most careful public servant and he could not look after the finances of the country more carefully if they were his own; every penny he has charge of is a prisoner. He is honest, he is sincere, he is loyal to his chief, no matter who that chief may be; and he works during the session fourteen, fifteen and sixteen hours every day.
Like members of parliament.

Perhaps. I would add this
on behalf of -the deputy minister. I believe there is no department where more free advice is handed in than the Department of Finance. Every day some person comes along telling us how to run the finances of the country, and the deputy minister gives a very sympathetic ear to all suggestions, and is always ready to listen to better methods of financing our national affairs.

Mr. Chairman, I
agree with everyone who has spoken on the subject in describing this as perhaps one of the most important subjects, if not the most important, which has come before us, and particularly before the Acting Minister of Finance this session, because it is very evident that year by year we are not only finding it difficult to repay our indebtedness, but that indebtedness is gradually increasing. This condition of affairs cannot go, on indefinitely. I would suggest that in refunding our indebtedness we should take into consideration the purchasing value of the money at the time the loan was made. Undoubtedly a large part of our indebtedness was contracted when a. dollar would buy a very limited quantity of goods, that is, when goods were at a very high price level; the debt is being repaid when goods are at a comparatively low price level. The result is that the individual or the country that made the original loan is receiving practically double the amount of money in repayment. This applies within the nation, and it applies internationally. As debts are refunded on the old basis, the creditor is receiving greater and greater value with the receding price level of goods. I believe that is our difficulty. Eventually I presume most of our indebtedness must be repaid in goods in one form or another, if it is to be discharged at all. When we find that at the time the money was borrowed $100, for example, would buy 100 units of goods, and that now we have to pay 200 units of goods in discharge of that $100, it is evident that the situation becomes almost impossible.
Under those conditions might it not be advisable to have such an inflation as would lead us back to. the price level existing at the time when .the debt was incurred?

I have considered that point a little. I do not pose as a financial or economic expert, I simply see the problem, and I concede that if you could bring about inflation to that extent, and could then pay off your indebtedness, it would undoubtedly be an advantage to you. Whether that would be possible or not is a very different matter. As I understand it, many of the debts were contracted in purchasing credits, especially as between one country and another, so that the loan was actually paid in goods. Therefore the individual or country that loaned the money originally is actually being repaid twice over. I am quite aware that it is impossible for every government to say:	"We will reduce the refunding amount so that it equals in

Refunding Loan
approximate value the value of the loan at the time when we received it," because that amounts practically to repudiation of the obligation. But I do believe that in the interests of ourselves, and in the interests of the nations, the time will come, and the sooner it comes the better, when a real economic conference will have to be called together to study suggestions for the refunding of indebtedness. This conference should be composed of representatives of the various interests concerned, of those who loaned the money and those who, through taxation, must repay the loan, and these representatives would eventually, I trust, be in a position to recommend an equitable basis of settlement. Because, frankly, Mr. Chairman, as I study the subject year by year-and I admit that I have studied it much more closely during the last three years than I ever did before- I am concerned as to what the future holds for us in that respect. I am no alarmist, but I am alarmed when I consider what must be the inevitable outcome of this continual refunding with its corresponding increase of our indebtedness. I believe that the grave importance of this problem will be borne in upon every business man in this country sooner or later. I believe that eventually we will have to state our terms of repayment in the value of goods and not in the face value of dollars, so that the lender will receive back the same purchasing power which he loaned. There is nothing unfair in such a proposition. If a man loans enough money to buy a suit of clothes, in equity if he is paid back a sum of money sufficient to buy him the same quantity of goods he is fully repaid. This may be considered bad financing but to my mind it is sound financing, and I believe it is the only system of financing that is going to stand up in the future, the only system that will enable us to discharge our obligations. I am not suggesting that the Acting Minister of Finance should attempt to put my suggestion into practice now, but only after consideration by a conference on the lines I have indicated. I am convinced that this problem will have to be taken in hand, and the sooner it is dealt with and solved the better it will be for us and for our future.

Mr. Chairman, my sympathies go out sincerely to the Acting Minister of Finance. I appreciate that he has probably the most trying portfolio in the gift of the government: he is responsible for all moneys paid out and for all moneys coming in. It is for that reason that such debates as we are engaged in to-day are, in my opinion, the most important that can come
before this House, and I was very sorry indeed to hear the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) say that we were wasting time. All over the world debts are growing very rapidly. Europe to-day is in an awful condition economically and financially, and only two countries are realty holding their heads above water. France, as we know, with a national wealth of sixty billion dollars, has a national debt of sixty-eight billion dollars.
There has been some criticism of what are termed the unorthodox suggestions put forward in the course of this discussion. When similar suggestions were put forward two years ago many members walked out of the House. To-day I am glad to see greater interest in these suggestions, and I congratulate those members who have given them a very fair hearing. We can make a great mistake in being too orthodox; there comes a time when you have got to be a little unorthodox and explore new means and ways of doing things. If five hundred years ago people had discussed in parliament such things as the flying machine, the telephone, the gramophone, radio and the other wonderful discoveries which we now have, they would have been placed in asylums or in prisons. We have been following on certain lines of orthodox finance for a long time; to-day there is a very large school of thought throughout the world which realizes that the orthodox school of finance has got to go.
There is not the slightest reason why when this matter is brought forward even the Acting Minister of Finance should refer to r.ur suggestions as Russianizing our currency, nor is there any reason why other hon. gentlemen should refer to them as wildcat schemes. The minister does not seem to realize that thu small group in this House who are putting forward these suggestions are his best friends. Unfortunately he does not appear to think so. But coming back to the main question. I understand that to-day the annual interest on cur national debt amounts to just about as much as the entire yearly cost of running the country previous to the war! That is something we have to recognize as a very serious subject to consider. I was much pleased with the way the hon. member for Red Deer ''Mr. Speakman) handled this subject a few minutes ago. This country is suffering under a tremendous load of taxation, and one of the reasons is that we have to-day bonds issued exempt from taxation to the amount of $931,312.900. It is because of these things that we are very anxious to help the Acting Minister of Finance cut down expense and get money cheaper if possible. The Acting Minister of
Refunding Loan

Finance may not wish to accept some of the suggestions put forward this afternoon and this evening, and I do not blame him for not accepting them right off. But I have something to suggest which is along more orthodox lines which I trust he will consider. He led the House to believe this afternoon that the loan that is going to be made will carry interest at 5 to 5h per cent.
No.

I shall be glad to be
corrected if I am wrong.
' Mr. ROBB:	I made no such statement
as to the rate of interest.

Does the minister expect
to get it at less than 5?
Ido.

I am glad to hear that.
Possibly he does not expect to get it at less than 31. I was therefore going to suggest that we have an excellent way of getting money at 34 per cent, probably as much as the government wishes. If he cared to offer 3i per cent-or, if the minister wishes, 4 per cent

through the post office savings. Why not throw the gates open as it were, and let the money come in, with the guarantee of the government, thus obviating the necessity for issuing bends, the country would be saved many thousands of dollars in interest, perhaps millions.
I was glad1 to see the ex-finance minister (Sir Henry Drayton) take part in this debate to-night. He has seen fit not to take part in these debates in the last two years, though he knows a great deal more about this subject than I think he cares to give the House. I regretted the suggestion he made that any one thought for a moment of issuing paper to pay for a two billion dollar indebtedness at once. The whole thing is absurd.
I would like to quote just a few lines from a speech made by the Hon. Reginald McKenna, of London, England. He said:
If banks increased their loans and investments, the results would be to increase the aggregate amount of their deposits but to add nothing to their cash resources.
I quote that because the statement I made this afternoon was not accepted, I think, by some hon. members. Referring to the meaning and importance of monetary policy, he said:
One man may tefll you to increase it indefinitefly, and keep trade booming, but if you do, prices will soar indefinitely. You will first suffer innumerable social evils, and finally the extreme depreciation of your currency will greatly impair your power to trade. fMr. Spencer.]
That, of course, was the case in some of the European countries.
Someone else may urge you to reduce the amount of money, and bring down prices to the pre-war level, or to such other arbitrary level as he happens to think the right one.
That was done in this country, with this result-I quote from Mr. McKenna again:
Yes, and trade will remain depressed, and unemployment will be with you all the time. Moreover, the burden of the national debt with the higher value of money will become intolerable, and no chancellor of the Exchequer will be able to balance his budget.
I think it will be generally accepted that if the price level be unchanged, an increase in the volume of trade will require an increase in the volume of bank credit and currency, that is to say, of money.
I quote these few words because I think it is just as well when hon. members deal with this subject in a rather unorthodox way that we should be able to place before the House quotations from men in such high positions as the Hon. Mr. Reginald McKenna as one supporting the views that we hold.

It is very gratifying to
note the interest that has been shown by the discussion of this resolution. I am aware that the House is not prepared to listen to any academic discussion of the finance question. I have tried that before on one or two occasions and I am satisfied that most hon. members are not even interested and are pretty well convinced that the finance system in vogue throughout the world is the best that is possible. They are just as much convinced of that as they were that the Bank Act was the best bank act in the world last year. Fortunately for them and for the world a revelation of the weakness in the case of national finance has not been brought about so speedily and in as clear a manner as it was in the case of the Bank Act, but I believe that a similar awakening is just as surely coming. There is no evidence that the Acting Minister of Finance anticipates anything different in the way of financing from that which has been in vogue ever since Canada had any financing to do, the road being followed must lead directly to disaster not only to Canada but to all nations following the same course. What is the end of the road? The end comes when you cannot tax your people any longer to pay the interest on the bonded indebtedness, not to speak of paying the bonded indebtedness itself. A number of nations are almost at the end of the road now. We are fortunate in having been a new country with tremendous natural resources, so that perhaps we may on paper look a little better than other nations. But we are following exactly the same road and in proportion to our ability

Refunding Loan
to pay we are not so very far behind some of those European nations which have brought themselves to a state of bankruptcy. While I am not going to follow that point to any length, I think it is necessary to emphasize the fact that this parliament is complacently launching another $300,000,000 loan on the same old) basis, and in the same old way, in spite of all that has been presented to this House, in spite of all the evidences pointing to the wisdom of taking another course that come from other nations which are approaching financial catastrophe. I know it is a popular thing to say, "It is all very well to talk like that, but what do you suggest?" One or two of us make a suggestion, and then you laugh. I am prepared to say that it is very unwise for any one to make a detailed suggestion on the floor of the House in the circumstances in which we are now placed. Are we simply to go on blindly because no individual member can stand up here and give a detailed outline of a new financial system that will carry us into safety? Is there nothing we can do? Have we reached the last resort, and that to continue with a system that every one knows to be wrong? I want to make two suggestions, Mr. Chairman, both of which I believe to be practical. The first suggestion is for the appointment of a committee, which suggestion has been made, I believe, by another hon. member.

Being ruled out of order
in presenting another possible means of raising our debt, I am practically shut off and must look for another opportunity to put that practical suggestion before the House. However, let me point out one or two other things since I have been stopped on that angle. I
was glad to hear the hon. member for Red Deer press a very interesting and I believe a very important point. Surely if we are going to attempt to pay back our debts-of course it is impossible to pay them back, but as long as hon. members think we can do it I have no objection to their holding that joyous opinion-but if there were any serious attempt to pay our debts, then the point raised by the hon. member for Red Deer when he urged inflation so as to bring the purchasing power of the dollar to what it was when the debt was contracted is surely a practical one. I notice that the ex-Minister of Finance attempted to answer a suggestion made from this side of the House and in doing so held that the government could not issue its own credit or recognize its credit in monetary form, because in paying back their debts that way they would have so much money they would not know what to do with it. It seemed to me that the ex-finance minister actually thought he had cleared the field when he had made that remark, that there was nothing else to be said. I am sorry he is not in his seat, and I shall not in his absence say all I wanted to say of his reasoning on that point.
I will be satisfied to say that in my opinion it was not an argument at all, and if I did not believe that the hon. member who made it knows far better than that, and can do much better, I would not have as high an opinion of 'his statesmanship as I have.
I regret, Mr. Chairman, that what I rose to say has been ruled out of order, but I believe nevertheless that there is a better way, and a more practical way, of raising this $300,000,000 than by the method that is suggested in this resolution. I believe that to follow the old method of piling up interest and pyramiding our debts must lead ultimately to a crash. I believe that it is possible to avoid that, but that it is only possible to avoid it by adopting a method that has never been used before; and the necessity for adopting a method that has never been used before arises because of the fact that we are face to face with a situation that never confronted Canada, never confronted the world before. I say that to go on in the same way, ignoring a new set of conditions, ignoring the piling up of debts that never can be paid, is to acknowledge the inability of this parliament to face the problem that stands before us.
Is my hon. friend referring to a method that has never been tried anywhere before?

Certainly.
Refunding Loan
Nowhere in the world?
Exactly.
It has to be started somewhere.

That brings to my memory the fact that the finance question is no longer a Canadian question; it is an international question. We are following exactly the same method that Russia is following. Russia is thoroughly orthodox in her financing. She is on a gold basis, if you please, only she is much more reasonably on it than we would be were we to announce our return to that shibboleth. Russia's financial position is set forth in the financial papers.
Where does the hon. gentleman get his information?

From Russia. Where did you get yours, if you want to controvert it? There is no doubt in the world that Russia is on the gold basis. The point I want to make is that it is very difficult for any one nation to take a new course except all the nations, or the most important nations of the world, are ready to help and take that course also. Finance is an international problem, and that leads me to the point I wanted to suggest when I was ruled out of order on the second head and that was the calling of an international conference to deal with this matter.

Is the minister aware
of the proposal which is being discussed in the United States to impose a duty of six cents a pound on copper ore entering that country? The minister is no doubt aware that the entire copper production'of British Columbia goes to the United States, and if this duty is imposed it will have the effect of practically closing down all the copper mines of British Columbia. I understand at the present time the total production is something like 50,000,000 pounds a year, and that in order that a refinery could be carried on profitably it would require a production of at least 100,000,000 pounds a year. Does the government propose to do anything to meet this situation? I suppose I should not use the objectionable word "retaliation". I got into trouble for using that on a previous occasion, but it seems to me if this kind of thing continues the government will have to do something. I will be very glad to hear from the minister in this connection, because the people of British Columbia are very much interested in the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am aware that there is a discussion in certain circles in the United States with reference to the imposition of a six cent tax on copper. However, that has not gone into effect, and it is not likely that it will go into effect, because I do not think under the provision in the tariff which permits the President to take action anything will be done with regard to a matter of this kind. One could not help realizing that it would be a very serious blow to the

Supply-Mines

mining industry in Canada, not only in British Columbia, but other places where a good deal of copper is taken out. We hope to secure on the continent a market for our product of copper, but my hon. friend knows that it would not be well to be too hopeful at the moment on account of conditions there. A private member of course may talk about retaliation, but I fear that a minister had better keep away from the subject.

Does the minister really think he should talk in that way, no matter what happens? We have had a multiplication of taxes against Canadian industry and against Canadian agriculture; but the answer is that it makes it all the easier to trade here. Instead of any talk of retaliation on the part of Canada, if my hon. friend runs true to form, he will come down with a proposal to still further reduce duties on American importations into this country. I would never think that if he were a private member he; would talk that way. If we can sell no copper ore whatever in the States, and if my hon. friend will simply carry on in the way we are carrying on at present, that will be an additional reason for further reduction, and for further paens of praise to my hon. friend that another death knell to protection has been sounded.

I notice that a portion of
the item is for the purpose of investigating mineral resources or deposits in the particular sections where the investigations are being carried on.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The sum of $37,000 is for the investigation of mineral resources. That does not mean that we only spent $37,000 out of the total vote of the Mines branch, because all the geological work was being carried on by the department in the interests of the mineral resources.

Is the minister ready to
announce the new Canadian national fuel policy to-night?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

The session is getting
on pretty well.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It will have to be a separate matter.

I do not want the government to overlook [DOT] this matter. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) early in the session moved a resolution calling upon the government to put into force this new national fuel policy for Canada, and the
/Mr. C. A. Stewart.1
government in order to get rid of the resolution accepted it; so that it is for them to announce it. I have not bothered the government on the subject since. We have waited patiently in daily expectation of hearing the national fuel policy announced. We are asked to vote $200,000 more to the Fuel Board without any policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is not the Fuel Board.
The Fuel Board is being paid out of this. Surely we should have the policy, especially when the government promised to bring one down.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I may say
for the information of my hon. friend that this vote has nothing to do with this policy. It is for investigating fuels which we have in Canada, and the use to which they can be put. A national policy, of which my hon. friend speaks, is of a different character altogether. We are testing our own fuels here to ascertain the best methods of adapting them for use in Canada.
What has been the outcome of the peat investigation, about which we used to hear so much? Is there any possibility of peat being used?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That investigation was carried to the point where peat was manufactured and sold on the Alfred bog; a type of machinery was developed which could manufacture it quite economically. That investigation was carried on in conjunction with the government of Ontario and both that government and this department felt that the point had been reached where peat might be manufactured with facility. I will not say however that the work has been completed because I am afraid that some engineers would suggest that better methods might be used; there is one engineer in this city for instance who thinks that we are not on the right track. The method adopted at Alfred was air-drying, spreading the peat on the ground and allowing it to dry in that way. The manufacture of peat at Alfred was accomplished to the satisfaction of both governments and now it is a commercial possibility if any one wishes to take it up. At the moment there is a company trying to float bonds to go on with the industry on the Alfred bog.

I have not heard much
about the matter in the past couple of years. In this government's opinion is it a success or a failure?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The production costs were about $3.50 per ton at Alfred. The freight charges are fairly high and I doubt whether peat could be shipped more than 100 miles to come into competition with coal. As a substitute for coal however for the fall and spring season in Canada it is quite good and burns freely, and it sells at about the same price as coal.
Has it been used in Ottawa at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. There has been, manufactured a quantity of about 15,000 tons at that plant.

There has been a good
deal of discussion about the settlement of the coal question, and there is evidence on the part of the people generally a desire to use Canadian coal as far as possible. I know that at the head of the lakes, from Winnipeg east to Fort William and Port Arthur, we have been using for a long time with satisfactory results coal brought from the western provinces. The question arises as to the possibility of shipping that coal to eastern Ontario, and rather strangely, ,1 have hardly heard it suggested that the coal might be transported, not by rail entirely, but by water east from Fort William. I know of course that most of the boats that come from the head of the lakes carry grain, but I think there are seasons in the year when these boats might be employed carrying some of the coal of the western provinces to eastern Ontario. I should think that in discussing the question of the route by which this coal should be transported from the prairie provinces to the East there should be considered the possibility of conveying it by boat from the head of the lakes. To-day most of the American coal is carried part of the way to the western country by boat. Take for example the Canadian Pacific Railway; for a long time they have been using Pennsylvania coal which has been brought by boat to the head of the lakes and then carried by rail west. Why not reverse the process in the case of our western coal and carry it to the head of the lakes by rail and then by water transportation east. I do not know whether this possibility has been discussed but certainly I have never heard it mentioned; I have always heard the matter treated as though there were no chance of using that coal in the eastern provinces unless it were carried by rail all the way. The minister might very seriously consider the question of arranging for the carriage of western coal in the way I have suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I doubt whether we can point to any shipment that has been made in that way; but nearly all the men who profess to know anything about the shipping of coal, particularly of lignite which is desirable for domestic uses in Ontario, are agreed that transhipment would break up the fuel very materially. It is held that the transportation of this grade of coal in the one conveyance throughout tends to popularize the coal inasmuch as it retains its original quality; all the experts are agreed that to tranship it on boats would break it up to such an extent that it would become slack and would deteriorate too much. However, the method suggested by my hon. friend has not yet been tried, and one cannot speak with authority until that has been done.

That is true no doubt as regards lignite. But surely in the hundreds of millions of tons of coal which we have in the western provinces-our deposits taking second place, in the coal supples of the whole world, only to those of the United States

we have a coal which will not deteriorate to any appreciable extent in transhipment. Do I draw the conclusion from the minister's remarks that we have not in the prairie provinces a coal that can stand transhipment at the head of the lakes?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am merely saying that in all the discussion that has taken place so far with respect to the bringing of coal from Alberta to Ontario-I am speaking of the domestic supply-the two main fields that have been exploited are Drumheller and Lethbridge as well as, to some extent, Saunders Creek, west of Red Deer. The bituminous coal could be shipped anywhere in any kind of way; you could dump it as many times as you liked without destroying it. But the coal which the Ontario people are anxious to secure and which the Alberta people are desirous of disposing of is the lignite which is burned in domestic furnaces; and if that coal is broken up or slacked to any extent it is not so valuable. There is no doubt that the ideal method of transporting it is to ship it in the same conveyance from point of loading to destination. However, until the other method is tried one can hardly speak with definite authority as to how far deterioration will take place.
In view of the minister's remarks it might be well to ascertain how far it is desirable to handle some of that coal by rail and water.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The traffic, as hon. gentlemen know, is all moving in the same direction. If the coal were going in the
Supply-Mines

opposite direction to the wheat our problem would be an easy one, but the difficulty is increased a hundredfold by the fact that it has to be moved in the same direction as the wheat. There is a time, from the middle of May until the first of September, when there is a diminution in the rail haul of produce from the West and when consequently there are more cars available. Fortunately that is the time when the mines are at their lowest point of production on account of market con-tions. But would that apply to the lakes?

I agree absolutely with the suggestion of the minister. It is exactly what I am pointing out, that there is a time in the middle of the summer when, it seems to me, it would be possible to make such an experimental test as we are suggesting. We have our Canadian Government Merchant Marine, and a number of the boats are laid up. It appears to me therefore that it would be a worthy project for the government to take one or more of these ships to load western coal from the head of the lakes for Ontario points. Surely some of those western coals would stand transhipment. There must be a time when it is profitable for such coal to be brought east by rail to the head of the lakes, because to-day we are using much of this western coal as far east as Fort William and Port Arthur. All the coal dealers at the head of the lakes advertise western coal, and a considerable quantity of it is used locally. I believe that we have been too much oppressed with the belief that we must have anthracite coal for our stoves and furnaces. But in the last few years when there has been difficulty in getting Pennsylvania anthracite, and consequent high prices for it, the people at the head of the lakes and west have been using soft coal from the prairie provinces and from Pennsylvania. For example, Pocahontas has been used very much during the last year or two with very satisfactory results. If I may be excused for reciting my own experience, I had always used Pennsylvania anthracite, but last winter I used Pocahontas, with much more satisfaction than I ever got out of anthracite. Pocahontas is, of course, an American coal, but I believe that in the western prairie provinces we produce coal at least equal in heating value to Pocahontas, and it is claimed that we produce practically an anthracite coal. So it .would appear to me to be a very worthy proposition for the minister to take into consideration the feasibility of bringing forward some of our western prairie coal by rail to the head of (he lakes for transhipment by boat to easivn Ontario points.
rMr. C. A. Stewart.]
It would also appear to me to be worth while considering the advisability of bringing coal from the section familiar to my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald). Nova Scotia coal could be shipped by boat to central Ontario points. During the past year or two we have been using Welsh anthracite, which is a very satisfactory coal from what I have heard, and surely if we can afford to bring over Welsh anthracite for profitable use by the people of Ontario, it must be feasible to supply the same market with Nova Scotia and western prairie coal. I submit that the minister would be acting very wisely as a representative of the government if he used some of our government mercantile marine ships for trial shipments in the way I have suggested, with a view to our being able to dispense with American coal which we are importing in such large quantities at the present time

Mr. Chairman, I am very sympathetic with the views expressed by my hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) in regard to utilizing our own coal supplies as far as possible. Curiously enough, our coal fields are placed at either end bf the Dominion, and for years the central part of Canada has relied on the United States for its fuel supply. The stringency that has arisen of late years in the anthracite supply from the United States has given rise to the idea which my hon. friend has expressed. I hope it will be found possible to carry out his suggestion, but I want to point out to him a difficulty in respect of the proposition which he makes to my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) to bring coal to the head of the lakes for transhipment by boats of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine for central Ontario points. The cost of carrying coal in steamers which are not specially fitted for the purpose becomes so great that the price of the coal to the consumer will be prohibitive. The Nova Scotia coal which supplies the St. Lawrence river market is shipped in boats specially fitted for the reception and discharge of the cargo by the most modern equipment, so that the cost is reduced to a minimum. I understand that the subject has been gone into by those in eastern Canada who are interested in the cheap transportation of Nova Scotia coal, and their opinion is that none of our government merchant marine boats have the requisite facilities for the carriage of coal.

What is the difference
in their build that makes them unfitted for this traffic?

Supply-Mines

It is not
so much a question of build as of equipment. The steamers which carry coal fron: Nova Scotia up the St. Lawrence were all constructed in England and are equipped with the most modern facilities for loading and discharging their cargo. This results in reducing the cost of operation to a minimum. The whole thing is a question of cost; unless you can put your coal into a boat and take it out again at a figure so low that the consumer is not going to be taxed abnormally in the price he pays, then water transportation ceases to be a factor. Then again there is the difficulty of bringing coal two thousand miles to Fort William, dumping it into ships and taking it out again, which means three or four handlings of the coal before it reaches the consumer. But if it be possible to work out a system by which coal could be dumped into a freight car at Alberta and brought direct to the point of delivery in Ontario, you would have a feasible proposition.
Mr. MANION. I appreciate the remarks of the hon. minister. At the same time I have been watching coal handled at the head of the lakes for the past twenty-five or thirty years and I have noticed nothing very difficult about it. All it amounts to is this,-the freighters carry wheat east as a rule and coal west, and they are simply large boxes, with no special apparatus except a derrick operating clam buckets. Any steamer may be used for shipping coal so long as it has open holds. Take for example the American coal which is shipped from the Pennsylvania mines to the head of the lakes and west, even up to the present time much of that coal is taken up in the large freighters which come east with grain

That is
anthracite.

Not only anthracite, but
a great deal of soft coal, too. It is dumped into these boats for Fort William or Port Arthur, taken out by the clamshell buckets, dumped on the docks and there transhipped to trains and carried west. A Canadian Pacific official told me one time that it had been taken west quite a few miles past Winnipeg to be used by the Canadian Pacific.

They do not use
anthracite.

No, the engines use the
bituminous coal, but it is Pennsylvania coal, and there is no reason why western coal should not be dumped into these same shell boats and shipped east, or why Nova Scotia coal should not be brought by the same type of
boat to central Ontario. The only difficulty would be in the canals, and there are small boats of the scow type which could be used for that purpose. During certain seasons of the year, as suggested by the minister himself, when the coal mines are working at their lowest and the steamships have the least to do, coal might be shipped from the prairie provinces to the head of the lakes, dumped into some of these boats such as the ones that now handle coal, and unloaded at Toronto or other points where they have the appliances for unloading. It might be worth while considering the possibility of doing something of this kind so that we can use our own Canadian coal instead of the large quantities of American coal that we have been importing during the last few years.

I am very
much in sympathy with my hon. friend's idea, but the whole difficulty is one of cost. American coal can be delivered on board ship at lake Erie ports at $2.50 a ton and carried to Fort William; it can stand the extra handling and the extra cost of handling.
What is the answer about Welsh coal?
That comes from England, and on account of the depreciated currency there it is produced at a lower figure than coal can be produced in Alberta or Nova Scotia.

Does that come as ballast
too?

It frequently comes as ballast. On the other hand the initial cost of the coal that comes from Drum-heller or Lethbridge, put upon the cars, is at least $4.50 a ton as compared with $2.50 on board ship at lake Erie ports. My hon. friend's idea is a good one if he does not want to break bulk at Fort William. If some assistance could be given, as was asked by the Alberta government, so that the coal could be transported to London, Toronto or Ottawa by one continuous passage in a car, we might accomplish what my hon. friend desires. But the extra cost of two or three handlings is such that the ultimate price to the consumer is very high. My hon. friend and I do not disagree; we aim at the same thing, except that I do not think the Alberta coal would stand the extra cost and the extra handling at Fort William.

I am told that coal can be handled from the Pennsylvania mines right up to the Great Lakes at a boat freight of 50 cents a ton.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The boat
freight is less than that.

Well, say 50 cents; it is
a small amount anyway. I see no reason why the same rate should) not apply eastward, because many of these boats during the summer go, one way or the other, light. Since that coal be hauled to the head of the lakes at this rate, it might very well be considered whether it could not be handled at a dollar a ton and transhipped east. The whole discussion of this coal question seems to be based upon the possibility of the handling of coal east entirely by cars, but it is claimed by those who have studied the question much more than I have that freight rates by water are about one-sixth to one-tenth the rates by rail. From the head of the lakes east is a thousand miles and that would make quite a difference in the cost of handling the coal east.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That has all been under consideration.

I have never seen it discussed. I have heard the whole rail haul discussed, but if we can get traffic going from Nova Scotia to central Ontario and from the prairie provinces to central Ontario we could handle that coal in such quantities that the cost of handling might be very materially reduced.

Will this Alberta coal not
stand shipment as well as the coal produced on Vancouver Island? We ship bituminous coal from Vancouver down to tidewater, a distance of 10 or 14 miles, where it is dumped into bunkers and shipped to San Francisco. That business has been carried on for quite a number of years. British capital is very much interested in the Alberta fields and is ready to invest provided this coal can be placed in Ontario at reasonable cost. Has the department been carrying on; experiments along this line and can we expect any information as to whether that is possible in the near future?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is
10 information to be had, it is simply a question of freight rates, the cost of carriage. The coal we have been discussing is lignite, vhich breaks down rapidly under exposure or otherwise, and that is the coal that is taking the place of the Pennsylvania anthracite. Bituminous coal can be shipped and transhipped fifty times without its being destroyed, but it cannot be used for domestic purposes.
[Mr. Manion. 1
We use it entirely in British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I know, but it is not used here. In Ontario we have been experimenting-in fact, we have almost passed the stage of experiment-in the converting of bituminous coal into coke. In this coke you have an ideal fuel to take the place of anthracite. Transportation costs are a very important consideration in the production of coal. As has been pointed out, coal can be landed at lake Erie ports at $2.50 a ton, and that coal will readily convert into a high grade coke at about $12 a ton. So that coke may in central Ontario very largely take the place of anthracite. Nevertheless I think there is quite a market for the high grade lignite fuel of Alberta as far east as and even east of Fort William, possibly into the Sudbury region and northern Ontario.
And Toronto?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I doubt
whether the transportation costs would make its use in Toronto possible. However, that remains to be seen.

Years ago I
heard the then Minister of Railways and Canals say that a solution of this problem would be through the canalization of the country from lake Superior to the foot of the Rocky mountains. That is a very big proposition, but he had it all worked out. He said it was feasible and that it would be applicable to the transit of grain. If it is applicable to the transit of grain and would save money, it would be much more applicable to the transit of coal from the prairie provinces. I think the minister would not be going out of his way if he took that matter up with the Minister of Railways.
That was the Minister of Public Works.

I quite appreciate what has been said with reference to the coking of coal. In my constituency, and in many parts of New Brunswick, there is unfortunately altogether too much use of anthracite coal, which is imported. We have large quantities, some in our own province, but on the whole a better quality in the province of Nova Scotia, of soft coal, which, of course, is not so desirable for use in homes, but which as the minister suggests is really the remedy if we could have something done in the way of coking that coal. We would then have a material quite equal to anthracite, and above all, it will be our own material, employing our own people,

Supply-Mines
and our money will be kept within our own Dominion. What I would like to ask is whether the government has any definite policy with reference to inducing the undertaking by any person of this process of coking. I can well appreciate the fact that many people will say:	Oh, that should be left to private initiative; let it be a commercial experiment. I am inclined to think it needs something more than that, and I would like to see the activities of some department of the government back of it in order that something will be done to induce people to undertake the coking enterprise and get it on its feet. All it needs, I believe, is to get a start and it will be successful, and I believe one of the purposes for which government exists is to give a start to get a development and really to point the way to opportunities. I would like to be assured that something of that kind is being done or will be done.

I am glad to hear the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter) take up this question, which has been more or less near to my heart for the last three or four years. I think there should be some governmental assistance, by bonus or otherwise, for the purpose of initiating in this country the process of manufacturing coke to take the place of American anthracite, which has been dominating the coal market in this country for many years. I am rather of the opinion that we have passed the experimental stage in this country. We know what coke is, and how it compares with anthracite. I would like to point out to the committee that we are being asked to-night to vote $10,000 for transportation charges from outlying provinces on ore shipments which may be sent to the Ore Dressing Plant, I presume here in Ottawa. In the same vote, we are asked to vote an item of $40,000 for publications, English and French, regarding coke and coal. I think we have had all the experiments we need, and it strikes me as very peculiar that we should spend on publications and literature on a question on which there has been much education already, four times the amount that we are spending on transportation charges from the outlying provinces, for the testing of ore shipments.
My hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River has brought up the question regarding the transportation of coal in our merchant marine. I happen to know something about the transportation of coal, and I feel certain that the boats of the merchant marine will not be able to transport coal at fair freight rates, as they are not equipped for that purpose. They are equipped for carrying various kinds of freight and wheat, although I am not sure they are equipped for even that.

They are equipped for
carrying both wheat and coal. To carry coal it is only a matter of having holes to dump it in.
I rather disagree.
I have seen it carried that way for thirty years.

I have seen them carry
coal for thirty-five years, and a certain equipment is required on coal carrying boats. Equipment is necessary, for instance, to unload the coal from the boat to the pier.

You are not up-to-date
down1 there. We do not handle it that way at all.
We are so up-to-date that we are carrying coal from Sydney to Montreal cheaper than any other transportation company; by "we" I mean those interested in coal.

You should bring it further
west.
I agree that something should be done to bring Nova Scotia coal into central Ontario and Quebec.
What about the St. Lawrence improvements?
And the Georgian bay canal?

I must leave my two hon. friends to discuss the relative merits of those two projects. As a matter of fact, we have no Georgian bay canal, and we have no deep waterway on the St. Lawrence as far as Toronto at the present time.

The United
States have a big prqposal before us now.

But it is not effective at the present time. We have all the coal we need in this country, East and West, more than we can use for three or four generations to come, and I think the government should grapple with this question in a broad and statesmanlike manner. It has been in the forefront of Canadian politics, for it is more or less a political question, for the last several years, and we have had experiments until I am getting tired of them. I want to see something done now. I want to see the Department of Mines, and if that department is not strong enough to take a forward step in this direction, I want to see the government of this country make this a national question. We are sending hundreds of mil-
Supply-Mines

lions of dollars out of this country into the United States every year for the purpose of bringing in anthracite coal, and we have in this country all the coal we need, and if this coking process was adopted, we could use our own coal instead of anthracite without much disturbance in this country, and I say that after having given this question some consideration. I think it is up to the government to take a forward ktep in this direction. I happened to be the chairman of a committee that took up this coal question last year, and we made a report to the House which was concurred in, but I have never heard anything about it since. I am not so very much concerned about that. Perhaps the report was wrong, but I want to say to the government of this country that so far as western coal is concerned there is only one solution to the problem and that is the question of freight rates. I have always taken the position, since we have had a Canadian National Railway, that it should carry that coal from the Alberta mines, or any other mines at cost in the West, to the central markets of Canada and in my opinion it would be good business if they did that. The present rate is $12 per ton but the railway granted a special rate of $9 or perhaps a little lower.
What about the possibility of boats carrying coal from the head of the lakes to eastern points?

The gentleman who did more towards developing a market for Alberta coal, especially in Winnipeg and points west of that city, stated in the committee that it would be impossible to compete with American coal on the basis of $9 a ton. The committee also went into the question of transhipping 30al which came from the Alberta mines at ;he head of the lakes. There is a certain kind uf coal in Alberta that will stand this transhipment; there is another class of coal that will not stand it. I believe the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) suggested at the last meeting of that committee, that notwithstanding the cheaper rates that might he had on the Great Lakes the cost of transhipment, would far exceed the rate of $9 a ton that the Canadian National Railways offered. That is all I have to say as regards the transhipment of coal.
Could we not depend on ;he Lake Freights bill to keep that rate down?
I have heard considerable discussion as to that but I believe in the long run the cost of transhipment would be greater.
Wait until we get our new bill through.

Coming back to the question of supplying the Canadian market with Canadian coal I consider there is only one solution of the question. First of all there is the problem of supplying the western area from the Alberta mines. In my opinion that is absolutely a question of the cost of transportation. I am one of those who believe that the railways of this country should carry that coal at cost; and if it is necessary to supply the Canadian market with domestic coal I would say the government should give them some assistance either by paying the extra cost that would permit competition with American coal-
That is good protectionist argument.
It is not protectionist argument.

I am not particular what my hon. friend calls it. I am a Canadiian and I want to see the markets of this country supplied with Canadian coal. I care not what my hon. friend calls it; whether it is a question of protection or a question of lower freight rates.
Nor am I very particular what my hon. friend calls it. We will let the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) name the policy.

The hon. member for
Hants, if the hon. gentleman will permit him to say so, is of opinion that it is a question of looking after the interests of the people of Canada. We are satisfied, if hon. gentlemen opposite will agree to cutting the duties off everything else, to let coal come into the country free. You people up here want all the protection leaving us in the Maritime provinces to be hewers of wood and drawers of water. Give us agricultural implements and other things free and we will be satisfied to have free coal.
The only protection my hon. friend wants is in Nova Scotia.

Well, we have not asked
for any protection in Nova Scotia.
Would my hon. friend (Mr. Manion) recommend an increase in the duty on coal?

No, I recommend the use of Canadian coal.

Would you recommend an increase in the duty? Answer the question specifically?
I am willing to try any plan that will result in Canadian coal being used instead of American.
Now, so far as our eastern coal is concerned-
Will my hon. friend tell me why it is we pay more for Sydney coal in Yarmouth than they do in Ottawa? To-day I am paying $12 a ton for Sydney reserve coal and in Ottawa it sells for $10.50.
My hon. friend is absolutely wrong. There is no Sydney Mines coal being sold in Ottawa to-day.

And there is no Sydney

Mr. Dawson of the
Purchasing branch of 'the Public Works department told me this session that he could get Ca.pe Breton-

That he could? Has he
got it?

-coal for $10.50 a ton
but down at the Rotary dinner the other day a gentleman told me he was getting Cape Breton coal for $9.50.

I am thoroughly familiar
with the coal proposition in Nova Scotia.

There is no such coal
as Sydney Reserve coal. There is Reserve Mine coal and there is old Sydney coal. "Sydney Mines Reserve" coal is commonly advertised by western coal merchants but it is a misnomer.

In answer to the hon.
member for Yarmouth and Clare let me say there is no Nova Scotia coal being sold in the city of Ottawa to-day. The coal that he has reference to is the Minto coal from the province of New Brunswick and that coal is being brought here at a little cheaper rate than the ordinary bituminous coal. The mine is practically on the line of the Canadian Pacific railway and I am told that in older to get freights from the mine to Montreal and Ottawa that the company carry the coal at a rate below cost and therefore successfully
compete with the bituminous coal from the the United States. That is the only way it can be done. I hope my hon. friend (Mr. Hatfield) will take my word for that.

The statement was

The man who said so
has been wrongly informed.

I should like to ask my hon. friend (Mr. Carroll) a question because I think he knows the coal situation pretty well. It is quite evident that the cost of producing bituminous coal in the United States must be lower than the cost of producing bituminous coal in Nova Scotia. Can my hon. friend say why that is so, or if anything can be done to remedy the situation?

I can explain that to

speechtext:
More than
that.

-is 'because there are some mines in West Virginia where miners are not used to mine the coal. Machines are employed to, burrow into the mountain side and convey the coal to the cars. In the province of Nova Scotia in some instances we have to go two miles under the sea in order to get coal at the present time, and I presume it is the same in British Columbia.

There are some places in
New Brunswick where you would not have to go that far.

I do not know much
about the mainland mines, but outside of the new mine just developed, at a cost of $2,000.000 or $2,500,000, by the British Empire Steel Corporation, the haulage is in the vicinity of one and a half miles and in some cases three miles. So that hon. members can see immediately why the cost of the production of coal in the Maritime provinces-and I am speaking of Cape Breton particularly-is so much in excess of the cost in places like West Virginia. I was informed a few days ago that they are developing a mine in West Virginia
Supply-Mines

where the cost of production at the mouth of the pit is 75 cents per ton. If that coal is on a line of railway similiar to those lines equipped by certain American interests, it is almost an impossibility to compete so far as Canadian industries are concerned with that coal in the city of Montreal or in any market as far east as Three Rivers or Sherbrooke. I am referring of course to soft coal. To my mind, if we are going to do anything towards supplying the Canadian domestic demand for Canadian coal, the question is one of coke. I think the experimental stage in connection with coke is passed. We know exactly what can be done in this country, and know exactly what coke plants will cost. We know exactly how many tons of coke may be manufactured from so many tons of coal, and, having knowledge of the cheapness of production in the United States, if we are going to have this question properly settled, we should have governmental assistance, and I am not particular in what shape it is given. I am speaking for the West as well as for the East. Recently I made a few remarks in this House, and suggested, after having given the matter some consideration, that the question for the West was cheaper freight rates, and the question for the East a matter of coking. I have always supported this government, and I am not criticising them in any steps they have taken; they probably know more about the situation than I do; but I am speaking from the standpoint of one who thinks that we have sufficient coal in this country to fill all the Canadian demands, and I ask why should we not utilize it? I believe every true Canadian in this House hopes that the day will come when we will not be sending $100,000,000 a year into the States, but that we will keep it in Canada; and make coke take the place of anthracite coal in domestic hearths in Ontario and Quebec. I think every fair-minded man will say that it is up to this government to take action; and perhaps it was up to late governments to do the same. Let us hope that the time will come when future governments will deal with this question in a national and broadminded way. If the government will do what I have suggested, I feel that they will have the support of every member in this House who thinks that we should have a Canadian market for Canadian coal and coke, instead of sending out of the country $100,000,000 a year, plus the exchange which we have to pay on American money. It might involve an expenditure by this country of $75,000,000 towards the maintenance of that market for Canadian coal. But even so, if that object can be attained, those of us who have in the 
last three or four years tried to proclaim this policy and to give the government some knowledge of it, will feel that we shall not have lived in vain.

I will give the House a
concrete illustration. I am living in St. John, New Brunswick. I would like some coke. I can get an occasional load from the gas works, but they do not produce enough coke to go round. The hon. member for Cape Breton vMr. Carroll) has shown us that it is a feasible proposition to make coke. We know that. At the same time nobody is manufacturing coke commercially. Has the government any thought of putting a government stimulus behind the coke producing proposition in the Maritime provinces? If they will translate their scientific knowledge into practical action, I think they will be doing a good thing for the country, and I will have no difficulty in supporting such a proposition.

I thoroughly
agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) and the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter) in reference to the advisability of having coke plants in Canada. The method has been worked out and found feasible. It would be a great benefit to Canada if we had it as the corollary of the St. Lawrence waterway proposition. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) is here. Let him tell this House if that St. Lawrence waterway is not the solution of the proposition of carrying western coal to Ontario, and of carrying eastern coal to western Ontario via the St. Lawrence waterway. I ask the minister to tell the House and the country *what headway is being made, and what are the hopes of an early solution of the transportation question by the St. Lawrence waterway.

It is pretty late at night
to start a discussion of the St. Lawrence waterway.
It is the solution of this proposition.
If the St. Lawrence waterway were deepened, it would be a solution of the question; but it would not be a subject of discussion at this time of night.

I wish to carry the discussion back into Saskatchewan for a few minutes, because after you leave the Maritime provinces the first coal you strike is in the electoral district I have the honour to represent. I do not see any money being voted in the main estimates for carrying on experimental work at Bienfait, and I anticipate

that the item will come down in the supplementary estimates. I rose to ask the government just what attitude they are taking concerning the plant at Bienfait.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have so
many questions to answer now, that I do not know that I can remember them all, but I will deal with the question of the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Baxter) first. There is no question, as the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) says, that the experimental stage in regard to the manufacture of coke is passed. Nobody denies that, and I would like to say that the S40.000 vote which has been mentioned is not for the purpose of advertising the coke, but to advertise to the outside world our mineral resources, and to provide for research work, investigation and geological surveys. We put an expert on this work last year and he made a study of the situation in Port Colbome, Hamilton, Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa; I am not sure whether he did any particular work in St. John but I know from advice I have received thait there is a possibility of a moderate plant being operated there. But the first consideration, which is a difficult one, is the question of disposing of the by-products. My hon. friend speaks of the gas coke, but it is not to be compared with the product made for the domestic market which we are speaking of. Before that plant can be successfully operated it must be hitched up with the gas companies, because the reduction in the cost of conversion is largely consumed by the amount you receive for your gas byproducts. I think I may safely say that the conversion will be paid for by the sale economically of the by-products. So that where there is a population of 75,000 or thereabouts it is no longer a question of experimentation to establish a coking plant: if the community is equipped for the use of gas the other byproducts can be used acceptably. My hon. friend speaks of encouragement. Last year we spent a portion of this money carrying on the investigation, not for the purpose of proving that you could make coal but for the purpose of ascertaining certain facts and giving needed information to those who would invest money in the enterprise; because it must be carried on as a private or a municipal enterprise. All that information is available; no one needs to search for it. People know what the problem is in the various centres because we have made a 3tudy of the question. I may observe that there is a plant at Hamilton where a contract has been entered into for the supply of gas. There are
now before the government requests for encouragement, and the matter is receiving consideration; and assistance is also asked for in connection with transportation. I think the solution of this acute fuel difficulty lies in the conversion of bituminous coal into coke. Coke manufactured at Hamilton to-day, I will guarantee, is equal in value to anthracite coal; a ton of coke is equal to almost a ton and a quarter of anthracite in heating value. So that you have an additional value. I think it is safe to say that anthracite sells at $16 a ton, generally speaking, in Toronto and other Ontario points, and coke can be delivered at the door of the consumer at $12 a ton. You have therefore a reduction as compared with the price of anthracite, and in this respect you have done something very much worth while for the consumer. After all we must keep the consumer in mind; for hon. gentlemen who represent the city of Toronto would be the first to kick if you increased the cokt of fuel to that city. And that is the practical difficulty that we meet whenever we begin to talk about an all-Canadian fuel supply for Canada. An hon. gentleman says that the cost of coal in Nova Scotia at the pit mouth is $4.50 to $5 a ton. Well, similar coal 250 miles from lake Erie ports is produced at the pit mouth at less than $2.25 a ton to-day f.o.b., and that coal is placed in Toronto in the yards at less than $7.

If the United States produces the same sort of coal so much cheaper than we do, and if we are going to maintain a protective policy at all, why do you not put sufficient protection on coal and let us have the market for that commodity? We have to pay a duty on automobiles and other things to maintain the industries in Ontario,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not discussing the question of duties.
But it is absolutely apropos.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Taking
Toronto as a central point in Ontario, bituminous coal sells at less than $7 a ton; if that is the case and if you have to bring the same product from Alberta 2,200 miles either by rail alone or by both rail and water, you will see the difficulty that presents itself. And I do not see how you could bring coal from Nova Scotia except by water if it is to compete at all with the coal that is landed in Toronto to-day at less than $7 a ton. So that if there is to be a national policy for the
Supply-Mines

supplying of this country with an all-Canadian coal, with conditions as they are in the mining industry in the United States at the present moment, you will have to impose upon the consumer in Ontario a considerably higher rate than he is now paying for his fuel. We might as well face the question at once. I will be frank about the matter and say that in my opinion there is no way I know of by which an all-Canadian supply can be maintained except by making the consumer in Ontario pay more for his fuel than he is now paying. Perhaps he is willing to pay more, but we must face the question and tell him honestly that he will have to pay more. I am just as desirous as any one else, if you can show me how it is to be done, of creating an all-Canadian market for Canadian coal. But I do not know whether you will put the consumer in a good frame of mind by making him pay two or three dollars a ton more for his fuel than he would pay with the American product available. That is the problem we have to face in connection with a national policy of this kind. I do say however that so far as Canadian fuel can be used without increasing the cost to the consumer, and where transportation can be reduced to the absolute minimum, I am prepared to recommend assistance for our friends in the East who have a serious problem of their own. In the East they have deep mining which is expensive; and the same is true of Alberta.
I said to the coal miners there that if they were going to get down to a minimum cost in transportation they would have to reduce their production cost, which at the moment is $4.50 a ton. That is the coal situation in a nutshell ; you cannot secure an all-Canadian market for Canadian coal unless you make the consumer pay more than he is paying now. With respect to coking operations, I would have anything that might be done in that direction confined to Canadian production.

I have discussed the coal question before this session, and, as far as I could, exhaustively; and I rise now to make a statement with regard to the cost of coal in Nova Scotia. My hon. friend from Yarmouth and Clare (Mr. Hatfield) states that coal costs in Yarmouth $12 a ton. In behalf of the collieries of my county which produce as good coal as can be got in Cape Breton I will undertake to supply all requirements in Yarmouth and all the western counties of Nova Scotia at $5 a ton f.o.b. their vessels. I do not know where the difference between $5 and $12 lies; it may go to the middleman for all I know. I do know however that we are

mighty glad in Cumberland to get $5 a ton for coal; and in many cases we do not get $4.50 a ton at the mine. Why to-day we are selling coal to the Canadian National Railway Board for a maximum of $5 a ton-good coal, steam coal for use in locomotives on the fastest trains.
Mr. STEWART (Argenteuil); That is f.o.b. railway?

are prepared to supply a minimum of 400,000 tons of coal a year f.o.b. ship.

About what would the

Coal is conveyed from Cape Breton to Montreal for less than $1 a ton. I would say that the cost in small steamers or schooners should not exceed $1.50 a ton.
Say 90 cents.

As I said before, it is a remarkable circumstance, and we have it even within a few miles of the collieries in Cumberland, that coal which is sold at the mines for $4.50 and $4.75 a ton costs the consumer $9 and $10 a ton. But do not let us blame the producer of coal, because I will undertake to say that there is not a single coal operator in Nova Scotia to-day who is making $1 on his investment.
