subtopic: PROPOSED ENLARGED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE ON BANKING AND COMMERCE

speechtext:
Mr. ARTHUR L. DESAULNIERS (Champlain) : Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by Mr. Gervais:
That the sixth report of the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce be concurred in.

subtopic: PROPOSED ENLARGED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE ON BANKING AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the sixth report of the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce reads as follows:
Your committee recommend that the order of reference be enlarged so as to embrace the study and consideration of the purpose, organization and operation of some type of properly administered central or reserve bank.
The minutes of proceedings of the committee have been laid on the Table of the House, and therefore we can refer to them in the discussion of this motion.
The order of reference, the enlargement of which is now sought, reads as follows:
That the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce should be instructed to consider the provisions of the Bank Act with a view to recommending such amendments to the act as would better protect the interests of depositors generally and prevent similar occurrences in future.
The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) in committee moved the following:
That this committee is of the opinion that the purpose, organization and operation of some type of properly administered central or reserve bank falls within the scope of the reference; and that a subcommittee be hereby instructed to suggest to this committee the names of competent witnesses to give evidence on this subject.
As chairman of the committee, I had to rule this motion out of order as not falling within the scope of the order of reference. Whereupon the hon. member moved:
That the order of reference be enlarged so as to cover the study and consideration of the subject matter referred to.
This question is by no means a new one. Last year before the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce, and also before the committee on Agricultural Conditions, it was studied at length and a vast volume of information was collected, the evidence being afterwards printed and distributed to all members of this House. The federal reserve system of the United States has been in force since 1913, and in the interval many books have been written on the subject, a number of these volumes being available in the library of parliament. Therefore if the purpose of those who seek to enlarge the order of reference is to collect more information, I think it is futile, because such information is now available in the evidence which has been printed and distributed and in the numerous books on the subject in the library of parliament.
On the other hand, if the purpose of those who seek to enlarge the order of reference be the immediate consideration of the creation of a federal reserve system in Canada, I think it is altogether inadvisable. There are in this House and in the country to-day a certain number of people who find everything wrong with our banking system, and who would like to reform it, not by the ordinary course of evolution, but by drastic measures which would be in effect an actual revolution of the system. This frame of mind is understandable. Some of these gentlemen have attributed the unsettled conditions prevailing in their particular section of the country to the fact that there is no federal reserve bank in Canada. They have also noticed that several banks have got into difficulties. We
Reserve Bank

had the failure of the Farmers' Bank a few years ago. The Bank of Hamilton had to be absorbed. The Quebec Bank was amalgamated with the Royal Bank. La Banque National was absorbed by La Banque d'Hoche-laga. And the Home Bank failed. Hon. gentlemen say that if we had a federal reserve board or a federal reserve bank such difficulties as these would not occur. I say, Sir, it is a mistake. It is an error of principle; it is a wrong way of reasoning. The difficulties confronting my hon. friends in their particular sections of the country are by no means peculiar to those sections. The financial and economic difficulties that confront the western farmers prevail also in all the agricultural centres of the United States, and if I read aright the information appearing in the United States press the condition of the farming classes in the western states is even worse than that of the farmers in western Canada. Nor are these difficulties peculiar to the farming class. In the industrial centres of the eastern provinces, Ontario and Quebec, and in the eastern states, these same problems have arisen. Quite a number of firms other than banks have gone by the board on account of the contraction of credit and the shrinkage in value of various commodities which is part of the aftermath of all great wars.
When the question of establishing a federal reserve system first arose in the United States is was to meet conditions quite different from those which prevail in Canada. They had the unit system of banking, independent banks with no branches. These banks had neither an elasticity in their currency, nor the facilities of rediscounting and of mobilizing the surplus assets centred in a few cities for use in other parts of the country where they were more needed. Let me state the objects which were put forward last year as the main reasons why a system of rediscounting should be established in Canada. Before the Banking and Commerce committee last year the question was agitated, and it was moved that we should create in Canada a federal reserve bank the purposes of which would be as follows:
(a)	It is a hank of re-discount for other banks, or a bankers bank; available for credit to banks, either when there is a financial depression and heavy demands on a bank or on the other hand elasticity of credit when there is business expansion and prosperity. In this way very large banking capital is less important in the banking system and there is greater stability of credits.
(b)	Open market operations to check too sudden expansions or too sudden contractions, by the use of bank discount.

(c)	As a credit agent in international trade and commerce for a broader discount market for commercial paper.
(d)	To act as a bank of note issue for the government instead of, for example, the Dominion government handling its own note issue.
(e)	To act as the fiscal agents of the government.
(f)	To be constituted in such a manner as to enable the people of the country by the government and to the government's appointees on the board of directors, to have due regard to the best interests of the people's prosperity and financial welfare.
Cg) To act, through its board of directors, as a disciplinary body on banks which might be disposed to engage in questionable undertakings on a large scale.
(h) To exercise, through its board of directors, inspection in a general way for unusual financial operations of the member and other banks.

The hon. gentleman is
reading from the proposal which I submitted to the Banking and Commerce committee last year, but it is important for the House to note that the proposals he has stated here refer generally to the federal reserve bank system as operating in other countries. Of course he did not mean that the system exactly as it prevails in the United States should be adopted, but the suggestion was that some organization should be created at least to discharge some of the functions which the system discharged in the United States.

I do not think the hon.
member wishes to read the wrong part of the proposals. If he will look at page 255, under the heading "Operation" he will see a statement of the actual functions that such an institution should exercise in Canada.

subtopic: PROPOSED ENLARGED REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE ON BANKING AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite correct, but I do not believe that the quotation I have made conveys the wrong impression to the House. However, my hon. friend has made the correction, and I shall not enlarge on the subject.
The question was put in the committee last year to several banking authorities, who were asked to express their opinion. Sir John Aird, Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor, and several others were examined by the committee, and gave their opinion. May I be

Reserve Bank
permitted to quote Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor's opinion, in respect to the advisability of introducing a federal reserve bank into our banking system in Canada? In reply to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) he said:
Mr. Ladner, there is no necessity for a federal1 reserve bank in Canada in our opinion. It has been suggested before and the proposal apparently arose from the contemplation o>f the federal reserve bank of the United States, the main reasons for the establishment of which were the absence in the country of means whereby: banks could obtain temporary assistance to meet seasonal or other special requirements. Second: The banking resources of the country could be transferred freely throughout the year to the part where the need for temporary advances might from time to time exist. Canada is under neither of these disabilities. Under the Finance Act of 1914 banks in need of temporary assistance can and do obtain from the Dominion government that assistance, while our branch bank system insures an ample supply of currency at all times and places where it is needed for crop movement or other purposes. It has been suggested that the tendency of the Canadian banks is to borrow from the government only with reluctance. Similar conditions prevail in the United States with respect to borrowing from the federal reserve bank, and in England with respect to borrowing from the Bank of England. Is it not as it should be? The note issues of the national bank in the United States, being based on government 'bonds did not expand and contract according to the requirements of the country whereas we have as you know a very flexible currency under the Canadian banking system. This expansion is covered entirely and absolutely by the needs of business and works automatically and perfectly. It is safe to say if the present Canadian system had for the past half century obtained in the United States the federal reserve system would never have been established. I remember in 1907 I think it was a great banking authority in Europe saying the United States banking system was uncivilized and the creation of the federal reserve system was an almost distorted effort to create a wrong banking system. It was in existence so long it could not be abolished any more than our banking system could be in Canada and it seems to us the federal reserve system has accomplished its purpose.
Sir John Aird gave a similar opinion in answer to the hon. gentleman's question:
Q. What is your opinion as to the wisdom of creating a federal reserve bank along the lines outlined in the proposal which was filed?
A. I think I answered that just now. I do not think the time has arrived for that. I think that if this country develops and we get the population, the time will come when we will need greater banking facilities, either by the present banks increasing their capital or by the establishment of some such bank along the lines you suggest, but I think it is not advisable at the time because it would be a great cost and risk.
This year we have had the great advantage of having before the committee as a witness Mr. Pole, the Chief National Bank Examiner in the United States. The question was put to him in the committee whether he thought the system that prevails in the United States would be of advantage in Canada. The hon.
member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) put the following question to him:
Having them in mind, the Canadian system and the American system, and from your experience as an examiner, would it be advisable or feasible to adapt the American bank examination system to the Canadian banking system without changing the principle of our banking system to correspond with the principle of the banking system of the United States?
Mr. Pole answered as follows:
The federal reserve system has been of inestimable value to the banks of the United States in ways too numerous to mention. Primarily, with the discounting privileges which it offers to its members, it has enabled a large number of banks to carry on through periods of depression when it would have been impossible to obtain funds elsewhere, and which must have closed their doors with reluctant heavy loss to depositors; and while some members of the system have fallen by the wayside in spite of the facilities which the F.R. banks offered, the question naturally arises as to how calamitous might have been the situation had there been no such agency in existence- and to the world this will never be known, but to those who have been in close touch with conditions since its establishment, the facts are undisputed.
The federal reserve system is admirably adapted to the unit system of banking, but for a very small number of banks with a large number of branches to attempt to adjust themselves so as to fit into such a scheme would appear to ibe highly impracticable.
Under the provisions of the Finance Act it seems to be quite possible for any bank in Canada whose assets would be of such liquid character as to enable it to take advantage of any facliities offered by the reserve system, to avail itself of equal opportunity offered by the Finance Act, the operation of which is easy and inexpensive, and, judging from the manner in which it has been functioning, quite effective. [DOT] The choice in Canada then would almost appear to be between a federal reserve system coupled with a unit system of banks which change would involve untold difficulties, and a combination of the branch banking system coupled with the Finance Act, which seemingly is meeting every banking requirement.
That is the opinion of a banking expert in the United States who came to Canada, made a thorough study of our banking system and gave us the benefit of his opinion.

speechtext:
I can best answer my hon. friend by reading again the motion for concurrence :
Your committee recommend that the order of reference be enlarged so as to embrace the study and consideration of the purpose, organization and operation of some type of properly administered central or reserve bank.
I did not say that what was meant was the identical system that prevails in the United States. What I did say was, that the study and consideration of any kind of central or reserve bank would be useless, because all the information was at present available, and if the purpose was the creation of such a system as prevails in the United States then, on the strength of.the evidence now before us, it is inadvisable to do that because we have already in our banking system all the facilities which the federal reserve system offers to the American bank. The head office for each Canadian branch bank is in itself a re-discounting bureau. It is a federal reserve system in

Reserve Bank
itself because it has the required elasticity, and it can provide surpluses at any point where the bank has branches. In addition, the banks in Canada, under the Finance Act, have all the re-discounting facilities which the federal reserve system offers to the American banks. Furthermore, in the opinion of Mr. Pole, and in the opinion of the banking experts in Canada, the great bankers who were called to give their opinion before the committee, it would be totally inadvisable, very expensive, and would not result in any profit, to change our present system.
I wish also to draw the attention of the House to our system as it exists. The Bank Act, which is revised every ten years, is the charter of our Canadian banks. When the Bank Act is revised the Canadian banks at the same time receive powers to carry on for ten years, and it has been customary since confederation not to make radical changes in that act except at the decennial revision. It would tend to cause instability in our banking system if radical and fundamental changes were introduced into the Bank Act every year. We can very well amend the Bank Act year by year so as to improve it; but, I repeat, fundamental changes would be unwise and would create instability. Therefore, I for one object to the concurrence of the House in the sixth report of the Banking and Commerce committee. It would mean a loss of time for the House as well as a loss of time for the committee; it would be a useless expenditure of money to call witnesses and adduce evidence with a view to obtaining information; and it would be utterly undesirable that the fundamental principles of our banking system should be changed before the next decennial revision. For these reasons I deem it inadvisable to concur in the sixth report of the committee.
Mr. JOS. T. SHAW (West Calgary): At the outset I direct attention to the fact that the Banking and Commerce committee only seek an enlargement of the reference in order that it may have the power to study and consider the position, organization and operation of some type of properly administered central or reserve bank. I quite agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) that no one, so far as I know, has ever suggested the application of the federal reserve system of the United States to our present system in Canada. The motion before the House simply asks that the committee be empowered to study and consider some type which might be found applicable to the Canadian banking system. I agree also with the hon. member for Lotbiniere 248

(Mr. Vien) that it is not necessary for us to call any witnesses for this purpose. There are mountains of literature on the subject all of which is available; and I have no doubt that the committee could come to a conclusion one way or the other simply by a careful analysis and consideration of some of the evidence at hand.
In order to determine the advisability of making any extension of our system along the lines indicated by a central or reserve bank, it seems to me, we should have a very clear impression at the outset of exactly what our situation is to-day. It is unnecessary for me to remind the House that parliament is charged with the responsibility of furnishing adequate credit facilities to the people of Canada. In its wisdom many years ago- and I do not doubt its wisdom in that regard -parliament saw fit to delegate this duty to certain quasi-public corporations, subject to certain rules and regulations. These rules and regulations intended for the guidance of the banks are laid down in the Bank Act, which is revised every ten years, and sometimes more frequently as necessity demands. Under the terms of the Bank Act the banks have been given many special and important privileges. The providing of credit to the nation has been exploited-and I do not use that word in any improper sense-by the banks for the purpose of making private profit; the banks are entitled to that privilege under the act as it now stands. We have provided by the act that from month to month, semi-annually and also annually, the banks shall make reports to the Finance department, but that department have been of little value so far as checking up or making any careful scrutiny of these returns is concerned. I do not think that anyone, not even the Minister of Finance, will dispute that statement, because I have only to call to the mind of the House that in the matter of the Home Bank the capital had been impaired for some seven or eight years while the Finance department had absolutely no official knowledge of that situation.
In addition to these returns made to the Finance department, provision is made in the Bank Act for the formation of what is known as a central gold reserve. That central gold reserve, which was organized for the purpose of allowing the banks to expand their circulation upon depositing certain specified securities, is managed by four trustees, one representing the government and three representing the banks. Furthermore, we have another alley along which our financial affairs run, known as the Finance Act. The Finance Act of
Reserve Bank

Canada, which provides rediscounting facilities to the banks and the banks alone, is operated by the Treasury Board. The Treasury Board consists of five privy councillors of Canada, with the Minister of Finance as the chairman and the Deputy Minister of Finance as secretary. Strange to relate, this Treasury Board apparently has come to the conclusion -although I believe all modem economists take the other view-that the interest rate cannot be used as an agency in either preventing unwise inflation or safeguarding against unnecessary and harmful deflation. Another illustration will suffice to indicate that the operation of this (particular act certainly invites some criticism; I need only mention the fact, disclosed in evidence, that while the banks under this act can borrow money at the rate of five per cent, when the government goes to the banks it has to pay five and 'a quarter per cent. Surely that does not speak well for the efficiency of our rediscounting facilities. In addition to that, there is another direction in which our financial activities lead us. We incorporated many years ago an organization known as the Canadian Bankers' Association, and under the incorporating act we have given that association certain supervisory powers, delegating to them at the same time certain duties of supervision. And I need not mention that in addition to all these ramifications, unconnected and unrelated, we have a Post Office savings bank which invites savings from the people of Canada and which is operated under the Post Office Department. We have also a government savings bank; I do not know under what department it is managed but I presume it would be the Finance department. And then we have the Mint which operates under the auspices of the British government.
The Minister of Finance now proposes, and 1 think he is wise in the proposition, to superimpose upon this system an inspection plan under the direction of an officer to be known as the Inspector General of Banks. He hopes I think with some reason, to convert the Finance department from a mere undertaking establishment, in relation to banks, into something like a hospital clinic, so that the banks may receive treatment before their collapse, .with a resultant saving to the depositors whose position, it is trusted, will be one of much less peril.
That is the situation that exists to-day; and that, in combination with what the minister proposes, leads one to .the conclusion that our system has been something like Topsy; it has simply "growed." It is not properly related, it is not properly co-ordinated, if I may be

pardoned the use of that term. That being the present situation, the question is, what has any type of central or reserve bank to do therewith? In the first place I might remind hon. members that central banks are nothing new; the United States is not the only country in which there is a central bank. With all its various and diversified interests the people of the United States have undoubtedly found this central bank to be a very effective instrument to keep the country financially safe and to promote its industrial development. We find, too, that in South Africa, with the varied interests in that country, there is a central bank. The same is true of Australia and also of Japan.
We are not necessarily wedded to the United States scheme. But taking the United States system, let me just in a few short sentences indicate what it has meant, according to the authorities, to the finances and development of that country. First of all it has effectively mobilized the nation's reserves so that those reserves are available in the place where and at the time when they are wanted. One of the witnesses before the Banking and Commerce committee illustrated the situation very well, I think, in this way. He said that suppose you establish twelve water reservoirs and pipe them together, if there was a drain on any particular reservoir, naturally there would be a flow into it from the others, thus maintaining a correct balance in all parts of the entire system. Similarly, in the case of a financial system founded on that principle, a proper balance will be maintained in all parts of the country making credit available wherever and whenever it was needed. So I say, it is admitted everywhere that the federal reserve system in the United States has effectively mobilized the nation's reserves In that country it has also increased the elasticity of the note issue. That is not an important matter in this country, because some people consider that the note issue is, if anything, perhaps too elastic in Canada. In addition it has provided rediscount facilities, and that, of course, has made possible the mobilization to which I refer. Fourth, and perhaps most important of all, it has created an intelligent control, in the public interest, of the financial resources of the country. That has been achieved mainly by the use of the discount weapon. At the outset the federal reserve system in the United States was somewhat new and there was some difference of counsel as to the proper procedure. But, through a time of stress and after a period of strain, it has been found that a federal re-

Reserve Bank
serve system can so use the discount rate that unnecessary deflation and inflation, both bad for the country, will be prevented.
These are the fundamental principles, as I understand them, which operate in connection with any central or reserve system. Can any of them be applied to the situation in Canada? Certainly it seems to me that with regard to the rediscount privilege, we should have some effective and competent machinery to regulate the discount rate in order that we may prevent the tragedy alike of inflation and of deflation. That is not done now. I am not surprised that it is not done, because I think that with political management even the best of systems will no't necessarily yield the results desired. What we need is an independent board to take charge of this situation and, indeed, of other situations mentioned; a board which will be in a position effectively to administer the nation's resources for the public? benefit.

What does my hon. friend
mean when he refers to the discount rate?

I am referring to the rate of
interest for rediscounting purposes. We do not propose, as suggested by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) any revolution of the system; we propose an evolution of the system. We suggest the adoption of some permanent supervisory board which will gather up all these frayed ends of all of these disorganized and incoherent parts of our financial system that we have to-day, when we shall be able to work out of that system something like coherence and develop a system which will function effectively in the public interest.
My hon. friend (Mr. Vien) has referred to several noted banking authorities who, he claims, were opposed last year to the application of the federal reserve system to Canada. Those same gentlemen last year very violently opposed any inspection system. I am quite sure that their judgment on that point was wrong; as a matter of fact, the minister is quite confident that their judgment was wrong, because now he proposes to introduce an inspection system which, I trust, will be satisfactory for the purpose.
I do not propose to labour this subject further, there are features of the federal system and of the central bank system which, I think, could be applied with advantages to the system in Canada. We could create a supervisory board-I do not care whether you call it a bank; there is nothing particular in connection with the name "bank"-of skilled, competent financial men, men who have made a study of conditions in Canada, who would 248i
be able to operate all our financial system and who could make it work intelligently in the public interest.
May I point out in conclusion that this is nothing new in Canada, because I find that a former president of the Imperial Bank, as far back as 1914 after discussing approvingly the inauguration of the federal reserve system in the United States, used these words:
The time wild come in Canada and come early when we will find it advisable, yes necessary, with our growth and development to establish a bank of rediscount under the .patronage of the dominion government anc with somewhat similar powers to those that have beet granted to the reserve banks of the United States.
Was that not quoted before the establishment of the Finance Act?

I think it was.. This statement was made on the 28th May, 1914. I quote it for the purpose of showing that the then president of the Imperial Bank realized the importance of adopting some of the essential features of the American federal reserve system.
Precisely what the government realized itself in bringing the Finance Act into vogue.

Yes, the government was
forced, by reason of necessity, subsequently to introduce the Finance Act as a war measure; but the president of the Imperial Bank spoke when there was no suggestion at all of a war or a pending war. Then I find that in 1918 a former president of the Royal Bank used these words:
In my opinion the question of .providing supplementary banking facilities in this country is very important and should receive the consideration of the government and the banks. If we had a bank of re-discount patterned somewhat after the federal reserve bank in the United States, it would render legitimately available millions of assets in the form of high-grade .commercial paper, now lying dormant in the portfolios of the banks, and thereby increase our financial resources. I think the government should appoint a committee of experts to investigate the suggestion.
That was said after the Finance Act was passed.

We should not close any
avenue of study or consideration which may be of profit to us in putting our banking system on a solid and safe foundation. Our banking system, if it is to function at all, must not only secure, but merit the confidence of the people of Canada.
4 p.m. That confidence unfortunately, has been sadly shaken, and it is our duty to leave no field unexplored where we may be able to find something of value which will add strength and solidarity to this system.

speechtext:
Mr Speaker, I should not like this
motion to go through without offering some views. I am very much interested in the discussion on the part of my hon. friends who have made a special study of the banking system of Canada, but there is no good reason why, at this stage of the session, we should enlarge the reference and refer this back to the Banking and Commerce committee. The committee made a very careful study of the banking situation last year; they carefully reviewed all the arguments for and against and, as has been so well stated by the chairman, the hon. member for Lot-biniere, there are mountains of information in the records. Therefore, there is no good reason why we should refer the matter back.
As regards the other argument just presented by the hon. member (Mr. Shaw) as to the advantages of a rediscount system, the present act under the Finance Act has been demonstrated to be quite sufficient for the requirements of the country. It works well and is well suited to the Dominion of Canada, even on the argument of my hon. friend. Under the Finance Act the people of Canada are getting proportionately just as much revenue as the people of the United States will under their federal reserve system. So that for that reason no good purpose can be served by referring the matter back. For all those reasons at this time I shall have to vote against the resolution.

As one who has been greatly interested in this subject, having given a little study to it, I think the report of the committee which the House is asked to adopt involves a determination of principle. The government should consider this point. The principle involved is whether parliament is disposed to allow the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce to investigate the advisability of a central or reserve bank system as now opera ted in other parts of the world; or whether parliament is to deny any such inquiry by the committee. I am not suggesting that we spend a lot of money in calling witnesses from all over the world. I quite agree that we have already accumulated much evidence on the subject and that we have an abundance of material available in the -parliamentary library, as we-ll as the experience of those hon. members who have been investigating the subject. But, in view of the conditions revealed in the Home Bank failure, the fact must be plain to all of us that unless our public men co-operate in a spirit of goodwill with those vitally interested^-our bankers

-in a thorough study of the subject, we shall be faced with such a situation ten years hence as every hon. member here will regret.
The two outstanding facts to-day in relation- to our banking system are, first, the tendency towards the elimination of our smaller banks; and, second, the .resultant centralization of the banking business in- the larger banking institutions. I do not say this by way of reflection upon our larger -banks, because I believe all Canadians should be proud of the way they have functioned, but to draw attention to the Jbald -fact that seventy per cent of our deposits are in the four largest banks, while the ten small banks have only the remaining 30 per cent, and thus are at a disadvantage in not being able to reduce their rate of overhead expense. Then there is the marked decrease in the number of our banks from 36 in 1910 to only 14 to-day. And, finally, we have the failure of the Home Bank and other incidents in- connection with our banking system which- have tended to shake the confidence of the public. Surely the mere mention of these outstanding facts is sufficient to convince any hon. member that it would be altogether inadvisable to postpone an exhaustive study of the merits of a central or reserve bank system. There is no desire to apply-in the words of the hon. chairman of the committee (Mr. Vien) -"revolutionary" methods; all we desire is that the committee be not denied the right to study this exceedingly important matter.
Does my hon. friend sincerely believe that if the order of reference were enlarged, the committee could study the question thoroughly between now and the end of the session?
No, not at all.
Then, what is the use of proceeding further?

But I do believe it would be a frank and wholesome expression of opinion on the part of hon. members that they desired to have the subject studied. In other words, the principle would be established. That is what I referred to in my opening remarks.

My hon. friend says that the
com[mittee should have an opportunity to study the question further. Any hon. member is quite free to give it further study. But the report of the committee in which concurrence is now moved is that the -o/rder *of reference be enlarged and that the committee be instructed to study -the purpose,

organization and operation of some type of properly administered central or reserve bank. dear. We have involved here a question of principle, whetheir or not parliament shall give authority to the committee to inquire into and study this question. Is not the hon. member
for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) aware that on May 21 the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce asked that this motion be put before the Houss; and does he know how it is that only now have we a chance to discuss it?

I think that question
might be more properly put to the chairman of the committee. I know we made the request in good time, in fact I had the honour of moving the resolution referring the question to the House, and I have been rather surprised that iit has not been brought to the attention of the House before. But, Mr. Speaker, I wish to appeal to hon. members to consider the real issue involved as I view it. Is the banking system of this country such that the members of this House should not make any further study of it in the committee; or should this House give the committee an opportunity of proceeding along the lines requested? That, in my judgment, is the question, and I hope the House will grant the application of the committee.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) in criticising the suggestion of a central bank of re-discount referred to the evidence of several gentlemen who were before the
Banking and Commerce committee a year ago, and pointed out that they rather criticised the suggestions then made. These same gentlemen in giving evidence before the Banking and Commerce committee at that time also stated that Canada had the best banking system in the world; that depositors were no doubt absolutely secured and that the banks were on a sound basis. I have only to refer to the history of such banks as the Home, Hamilton, Banque Nationale, and others of which we all know, institutions that have been through very trying times since those statements were made. I simply mention that to show that if those gentlemen were wrong in the second statement they made, they probably were wrong in the first.
The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) mentioned that a very thorough study was made of these questions a year ago. That is correct, but unfortunately, although we took a lot of evidence in the committee on various sides of this financial question, nothing has been done, no action has been taken with respect to same.
Did any discussion take place in the committe last year on the proposals submitted by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner)? I do not remember any.

The only evidence was
that given by the hon. member for Vancouver South.
In the remarks that I shall make this afternoon I wish largely to review the question of note issue. The issue of bank notes is referred to in section 61, subsection 2 of the Bank Act: Banks are allowed to issue up to the amount of their paid-up capital as a special privilege to those corporations. This was at one time thought to be sufficient for the means of exchange. However, the business of the country has so increased we have had to find other means of increasing the issue of notes. The first extension that I can find was made in 1908, when the banks were allowed during the crop season to issue extra notes to an amount equal to fifteen per cent of their paid-up capital and reserve between the months of October and January. Later they found that this was not sufficient and the time was extended from September 1 to February 29. This is quite a privilege to the banks. One will find upon looking up the figures for 1922 that the bads in that year had paid-up capital amounting to $125,500.000 and reserves of $129,500,000. It therefore meant that they had the privilege of issuing extra notes to an amount equivalent
Reserve Bank

to over thirty per ce|nt of their paid-up capital. I am commenting on this only to show that as business increased in the country we had to find some means of getting a larger supply of the medium of exchange in the matter of note issue.
I would like to refer, however, to the year 1904, when the paid-up capital in comparison to the total assets amounted to 11 per cent. Twenty years afterwards we find that it only amounts to 4 per cent; in other words, as business has increased1 the ratio of capital to assets has decreased. Other means also had to be found to create a sufficient medium of exchange, and in 1913 the central gold reserve was started. The central gold reserve, according to one of the men who had a great deal to do with starting it, was never intended to be anything else than a gold reserve where gold could be placed and notes issued against it. But the use of the gold reserve has wandered a long way out of that path since that time. In 1914 the Finance Act was passed, which made it possible for the banks to bring certain securities to the Treasury Board and obtain Dominion notes against them for a charge of 5 per cent. A lot of these notes were issued in large legals to facilitate inter-bank exchanges, but a large quantity was taken to the central gold reserve and placed there so that against it they could issue their own paper. We were informed in the Banking and Commerce committee a year ago that the reason they wished to issue their own paper instead of issuing Dominion paper was because of the matter of advertising. We have to-day in the central gold reserve, in round figures, some $9,000,000 of gold and some $56,000,000 of notes or paper. In other words, as a well known banker who made his name famous in Canada some years ago stated to me, it was really more of a gilded reserve than a gold reserve.
Regarding the quality of the securities left with the Treasury Board I would like to quote an answer given to the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) in 1922:
Notes to the amount of $87,115,075 were issued to the hanks as advances under the Finance Act, 1914, and secured by the deposit of securities approved fay the Treasury Board, including Dominion of Canada bonds and treasury bills, bonds of the provinces of Canada and Canadian municipalities, British Columbia treasury bills, Canadian Northern Company notes, certain industrial bonds and stock, assignments of grain and produce and demand notes of commercial houses endorsed by the banks to the order of the Minister of Finance.
You will notice that two of the items in this list were Dominion of Canada bonds and treasury bills. It is interesting to note

that when the government wants to borrow money from the banks it issues treasury bills, and to-day we have outstanding to the banks in treasury bills no less a sum than $91,315,000. You will notice, as mentioned by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw), that although we charge the banks only 5 per cent on the notes issued to them against the security offered,-which security might be treasury bills-we pay the banks themselves for money lent against treasury bills 5| per cent. These treasury bills can again be brought back by the banks to the Treasury Board and the banks can obtain Dominion notes against them at 5 per cent. Otherwise you might look upon it as a sort of looping the loop.
It is rather interesting to note that this privilege of going to the Treasury Board with securities and rediscounting them is open only to the banks. It is not even open to the provincial governments. It is what you might call a bankers' bank, and I think a good deal might be done to widen the scope of the work done by the Treasury Board. It could very readily be taken over by such an institution as the central bank, which is being suggested. I would like to remind the House that these treasury bills, which the banks hold at the present time to an amount over $91,000,000, run for only the short period of six months. Does it not seem absurd that the Dominion government, in making use of its credit, should not only have to go to a third party, but pay more money for its borrowings than it charges the same parties when loaning to them, and that these notes should run for only the short period of six months?
I should like to say a few words with regard to the responsibility of note issue. The private notes are the first call on the assets of a bank in case it fails. It is true that we have what we call a note circulation redemption fund, but it does not serve the purpose that the public for a good many years have been in the habit of believing it does. It has been the impression of the public that if a bank went to the wall, all its notes would be taken care of by the note circulation redemption fund. This, however, is not the case. The fund comes to the rescue for the time being in the shape of a loan, but the entire amount that a bank which has failed can call on the fund as an asset for, is the amount it has paid into that fund. This is contrary to what has been the belief of the people of Canada generally up to a short time ago, but when the unfortunate failure of the Home Bank took place we found that the bank had outstanding some $2,000,000 of notes, and that it had only

Reserve Bank
$100,000 in the note circulation redemption fund, and that was all it could call upon as its part of the assets of that fund. The fund was intended to be to all intents and purposes an insurance fund, but as it operates at the present time under the Bank Act, it is not an insurance fund at all, except to the extent that it is a sort of loaning agency for the time being, but the loan has to be paid back when the assets, including the deposits of the bank, are realized.
Before I sit down I would like to touch on just a few of the very interesting matters that have come before us during the last two years, in the banking committee, and some of these are rather startling, particularly when we remember that last year we were informed that our Canadian banking system was so perfect that we could not amend the Bank Act with any satisfaction to the public, and that therefore it should not be amended.
It is realized to-day that there is no government guarantee behind the deposits of private banks. It has also been discovered that it is possible for the entire deposits to be seized to meet notes outstanding. It has been the impression of the depositing public for a good many years that if they put money into a bank all they had to do when they wanted to draw it out was to issue a cheque on the bank. That is true as long as the bank is running, however bad its condition may be, as we have seen in the case of the Home Bank, which has been in a bad condition for the last seven years; but when the bank closes its doors, what happens? We find that the first lien on the assets of the bank is the notes; secondly, comes the Dominion government, together with any advances made by the Treasury Board; thirdly, the provincial government; fourthly, any secured creditors,-and in the case of the Home Bank we found that they had mortgaged their buildings to a firm in New York;-and fifthly, come the depositors, who otherwise are unsecured creditors. A bank may lend an amount equal to its paid up capital to any one concern. This was proved in the case of the Home Bank and La Banque Nationale. Under the present system that could not very readily be seen, and I hope it will be checked, by the Inspector 'General who we hope will be appointed during the coming year. The system might be made more perfect by having a central bank of rediscount, with officials working in co-operation with the Inspector General.
We find also that to-day sixty per cent of the banks'capital is in bank [buildings. To give
an idea of the way the banks have been reduced in number-very largely because the small banks under the present system, and in the absence of a central bank of rediscount- have little chance compared with the larger ones, we find that in 1919 Canada 'had 36 banks and to-day it has only 14. As the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) mentioned, four of our Canadian banks control seventy per cent of the total deposits, and the other ten control only thirty per cent.
A government central bank, in the opinion of many of us, should have complete control of note issue. This not only would relieve a great liability from the shoulders of the depositors, but it would be the means of bringing in a very large revenue to the government exchequer, and would relieve some of the burden now resting on the shoulders of the Minister of Finance.

I
want to say in the first place that when I undertake to criticise in any way the banking institutions in this country, my main hope in regard to them is that they make double the money they now make, and that they may give four times the service they now give for that opportunity of making profits.
I want to see the banks prosper, but the underlying principle of banking, the thing behind the banking of the country, must be, as it is in all the other countries of the world, before anything else, the credit of the nation. Banking has become absolutely a state proposition throughout the world. It is under the control of the state, it has the credit of the nation behind it, and the nation has the leadership in the banking of the country. That cannot be denied. It is the case all over the world to-day with the exception of Canada. In some way the private banks have got the leadership of banking in this country. But they have behind that leadership the national credit and they seem to control that as well as their own resources What we want to put behind our banking system is the nation. We also want the nation to have the control rather than the private banks and to give a banking service to the country at the lowest possible cost at the same time allowing the banks a reasonable profit.
Analogy is a poor kind of reasoning but let me give an analogous case. It is that of the railways of this country. Formerly private companies were in control of a great many of those railways and with the exception of one company they wrecked themselves and the country has to come to their relief, take over
Reserve Bank

the liabilities and the railways themselves and re-organize them into a great system of national transportation which to-day promises to be successful. The same thing, or a somewhat similar process, may have to be applied to banks because the banks are getting smaller in number, as has been pointed out here today, and they are becoming more of a monopoly. But the more they grow in that direction the more they wish to dictate the banking policy of the country. That should not be. The credit of the country should be behind the national banking system.
We have an example before us, and it is the one that makes the most impression on this country, the example of the national banking system they now have in the United States. I suppose I will be charged with advocating the introduction into Canada of the United States banking system. But that country adopted their present system after years of effort, after years of experience of great losses, after years of the failure of many banks. But gradually they have evolved a system which is satisfactory to that country, and the people of the United States would not change their national banking system to-day for any private banking system they had heretofore. They believe absolutely in the state being behind their system, and they insist on a national banking currency-a thing we ought to have in this country but we do not have. They insist also over there on a national system of bank inspection. We may have the beginning of such a system as that in this country but it was denied to us at the last session of parliament, and it was denied on the evidence of the private banks of Canada who do not want bank inspection. But in the United States the system of bank inspection is proving a great success, and it is weeding out the weak banks. Under their system,-the United States bank examiner has told us and we know it is a fact,-they can find out in three weeks whether a bank is sound or not. It took us eight years to find out that the Home Bank had been a failure, had lost a lot of money, and had been conducted in an improper way. Therefore what we should do is to study the proposition and see whether we should not adopt the system they have in the United States-a system of national banks and in connection with it a national currency.
I do not know who can object to this. We have a national currency but the effort of the banks is to make that disappear and substitute a bank currency which is not always reliable, which is questioned, and the retirement of which in times of trouble becomes a grievance to the country and a source of

much complaint. There is no question of the solvency of the national currency. Hon. gentlemen say, and they said before the committee to-day, that there is a redemption fund. But how is it administered? It is not administered well. It allows the currency to be questioned, and that being so when a better example is offered us, such as they have in the United States, we ought to adopt it. That is not the only instance in which the banks over there have a superior system. Their system of rediscounting is as good as ours, in fact it is a good deal better. It allows the credits to be moved all over the country by the organization of the National Reserve Bank system. Every bank there has to be a member bank of some reserve bank system. Consequently it is always under the inspection of fellow member banks who know whether it is sound or not. It it has gone wrong they find it out, expose it, and cause a correction to be made. Under the system of bank inspection there if losses have occurred they are found out and the bank has to make the losses good; if their capital has been impaired it must be strengthened. In that way the American system is recognized as being much better than ours and is considered better adapted to the country. We ought also to make a study of these things which study should lead up to the improvement of our own banking system.

So much the
worse for the Canadian branch bank system. We all know of course that we have in this country a branch bank system which is not perfect; but can we not make it a better system if that is possible? That is the issue. But the banks do not like to have any comparisons made that are at all to their detriment. They say, "Are we not giving you good service now? Do we not do this, that and the other?" Well, they do give us some kind of service, but that service can be very much improved. And in my opinion the branch system can be carried on successfully by the adoption of some of the improved methods which have been followed in the United States.
As regards the central gold reserve, I will not call it a humbug, because it is a substantial thing. But why should it not be in the control of the nation just as in the United States and in practically every other country? The central gold reserve in Canada is confined to Montreal, and is in the hands of the bankers, save alone that there is one representative of the government on the board. I see no reason, however, why the reserve should not be absolutely in the hands of the nation, in the national treasury, as in the United States. Once again I must apologize for advocating something which in the United States is superior to what we have in Canada; but I think we should create in this country, at Ottawa, a real treasury department, such as there is in the United States. In that country there is a highly paid national official, who has charge of the national treasury, who has charge more or less of the national reserves of the nation and of the note issue of the nation, how it goes out and how it comes in. He is a real national treasurer, not only for the nation in its organization as a nation, but for the whole country. He has control of the rediscounting of notes in connection with the federal reserve bank system. Who controls the national system? The national reserve,

and there are billions of gold in the national reserve at Washington. This is all done by the nation and without any idea of making money out of it. The national reserve at Washington looks after the national notes, and nobody ever questions the solvency of the national notes of the United States now. I remember, as a boy, just after the American war, seeing in Hamilton American national dollar notes sold for about thirty-five cents. From that degradation of an American note to that low figure, I saw it rise gradually to par, and now it is the best note in the world. The greatest amount of credit available for the world at large to-day is concentrated in the United States, and this is the gradual result of the creation of a great national system of banking based on the nation's credit. We want to do that in our country. If they have done it there, we may be able to grow in that direction.
Hitherto, nearly every critic who has come forward in this country to pass judgment upon any one who makes a proposal such as I am making here to-day, or as some hon. gentlemen who have preceded me have made, say that we are suggesting Yankee notions. The outcome of those Yankee notions is the creation of the greatest banking system in the world. I do not place even England before it, because England has had to come to the national banking system of the United States to take care of the immense national debt she created in the war. That question was settled and arranged at Washington, and England's debt is being retired at Washington. The United States, it is true, was in the war, but not to the extent that the Mother Country was and the national banking system of the United States is the organization the world looks to now to clear up the mad condition of affairs in Europe. It is the hope of the world to-day, if war is ever to cease and we are to get on our feet. If Germany is to be redeemed and put on her feet after the war, she must do her financing by way of the United States on the basis of the national banking system.
I have nothing to say against the banks of this country, which have done good service, but they are growing into a monopoly. Where is this going to end? I am not going to make any prediction as to what will happen, but I shall be greatly surprised if you do not see, in the near future, more mergers in this country. As the system is moving that is inevitable. There are four big banks and a number of smaller ones, and I do not know that the smaller banks can get along in view of the opposition of the four big banks. What
we want is to go back to the small bank. These are the ones that have made the failures, it is true; but if they were prohibited from making note issues against their capital, as they are allowed to do now, I believe the smaller bank system is what we want. We want local banks, organized by groups of local capitalists, to collect the deposits of their localities and to put them into local industries.

In 1914, when we went into the Great War, Sir Thomas White, then Minister of Finance, called the bankers together, and they decided that we needed something to bolster up the Canadian banking system, and that we had to have it in a hurry. I should like to quote a few lines from an address Sir Thomas White [DOT]gave in Toronto, referring to what he said at this meeting of the bankers held here in Ottawa :
We said to the banks: The Dominion government wild loan you in Dominion notes, which are legal tender, twenty-five, fifty million dollars; we put no limit, if you need it, you probably will not, but if you do, we will loan without limit on securities approved by the minister. You bring in high-class securities, or commodity bflls, because they represent their full value in goods, and we will lend to you at 5 per cent Dominion notes that will make you liquid, and you need not worry about your reserves. There was no more panic after that announcement was made. From that day to this there has been the utmost confidence in the Canadian banking situation, no sign of panic. That gave flexibility to our banking system, made our bankers confident that they could meet any situation that could arise, and, of course, they could give the puiblic very much more extensive credits than they otherwise would have got.
Later on he says:
It was the right thing to do, but no permanent measure followed.
In a recent issue of MacLean's Magazine I saw that Sir John Aird was quoted as saying that in his opinion the inspection of banks is not very practicable, and is not needed, but he would suggest that the Finance Act be made permanent. I would suggest to this committee that if the Finance Act is to be made permanent, surely we should have some sort of a permanent board to administer it. The act is administered at the present time by the Treasury Board, which consists of four cabinet ministers They may know something about banking, and then again they may not know very much. The next government that assumes office-and I suppose we will have [DOT]a change some day-will cause a complete change in the personnel of the Treasury Board and the new body will then have to administer the act without having the benefit of the experience of their predecessors. To show you how the Finance Act is administered, I will quote one clause from the act.
Such securities shall be deposited with the minister or with an assistant receiver general. The minister may request the trustees of the central gold reserves to make a valuation of and recommendation as to the amount which in the judgment o>f the trustees may properly be advanced on any securities offered in pledge under this act.
I am informed that the trustees of the central gold reserve are the Bank of Montreal, the Royal Bank, the Canadian Bank of Com-

merce and the Royal Trust Company, the last named being a subsidiary of the Bank of Montreal. That is practically placing the administration of the Finance Act in the hands of three banks and they are three of what are generally termed the "big four". Is that not creating a monopoly of banking in Canada? Why should the other banks of this country have to have their securities valued by three of the big four banks in this country when they come to the Treasury Board and ask for an advance under the Finance Act? Would it not seem wiser to have a central bank, with a practical banker at the head and a few experienced bankers under him, to judge the securities that are offered?

That act works like a machine in maintaining the rate of interest, at 5 per cent all the year round and 5 per cent every year. At the present time money can be borrowed in New York at rates as low as 2 and 2i per cent. Why would our banks wish to come to the Finance department at Ottawa and pay 5 per cent if they can go to New York, deposit securities there, and borrow money at 2| per cent? I have heard that is being done by some of our Canadian banks and I do not blame them; I think it is good business for them to do it. But I do ask that our Finance Act should be administered in a businesslike manner. If these banks can obtain advances in New York at 2i or 3 per cent why should not these trustees see to it that money is loaned to the banks at the same rate of interest? Mr. Fielding was quoting the sums which had been made I believe the exMinister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) observed "Yes, and it is all clear profit". In giving my reasons why I think a federal reserve bank or a central reserve bank-it does not make much difference how it is described-should not be grafted on to our banking system, it seems to me that it will be well to survey the basis of our banking system, because it goes without saying that if this system is not adaptable to a central reserve bank, it would be the height of foolishness to assert that such a bank should be established. Our banking system is based on what is known as the branch bank system of Great Britain, that is to say, a certain number of large banks each with numerous branches throughout the country. In contradistinction to that system we have the United States system, which is based on what is known as the unit system, each unit being independent and forming a banking entity. I quote the United States system because in that country they have a Federal Reserve Bank, which I will discuss later on.
Now, in the course of this debate the question has arisen as to the number of banks in this country, and this question has a bearing on the subject matter before us. We have been told, quite correctly, that we have fourteen chartered banks, and the opinion

has been, expressed that possibly this is too small a number to handle the banking business of the country. In this connection it will be interesting to make a comparison with the number of banks in Great Britain. There 80 per cent of the banking business is carried on by five large banks having over seven thousand branches, as compared with our fourteen chartered banks with over four thousand four hundred branches. This comparison, it seems to me, demonstrates that we have a sufficient number of banks.
In determining our attitude towards the question now before us it is important to understand the United States banking system. They have 8,000 national banks and 23,000 state banks, to say nothing of trust companies, private banks, and concerns of a semi-banking character.
Let us look briefly into what are the main purposes of banks in general. These are, first, the issuance of notes, in which of course is included security for the notes; secondly, the taking of deposits, in which of course is also involved the safety of the depositors; thirdly, elasticity of circulation; and fourthly, elasticity of credits, which of course includes privileges of re-discount and such like. All these functions are inherent in our banks and are exercised by them. But before dealing with these various functions let us see what the result of our banking system has been. the bank circulation fund all noteholders of defunct banks have been paid in full.

have suffered tremendously from these recurrent waves of feverish prosperity and intervening periods of paralyzing depression. This is something that has faced all of us, and the cause has now been discovered in an unregulated, unmanaged, happy-go-lucky currency. He has shown that the actual facts prove that the business cycle largely follows and depends upon the rapidity of fluctuations in the price level. It is a very interesting document that was published in the proceedings of the American Statistical Association in December of last year.
I have here another pamphlet by Professor Irving Fisher dealing with the same matter, entitled "Stabilizing the Dollar." This was published in Harper's Magazine in March of this year, and I think as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George has taken up considerable time, I shall quote briefly from this very interesting pamphlet for the benefit of hon. members. He says on page I:
From the beginning of things monetary mankind has been harassed by mysterious, periodic price-floods -both ebbing and flowing-comparable to the plagues of Egypt. We have always blamed the wrong man -the "gold-bug" if prices went down; the "profiteer" if prices went up. Yet both of these alleged scoundrels have been merely carried by the mysterious tide they were accused of consciously making. Within the past three years this tide has surged up and down in such quick and bruising succession that the real truth has begun to get itself knocked into a few of us. For who can now go on believing that mere little cliques of human beings whose interests are opposed could take turns at controlling the tides in opposite ways three times within a year! When, therefore, most economists, some business men, a few bankers, and a legislator or two begin to talk "unstable dollar", the rest of us may at least feel justified in taking notice. What has so long prevented the ordinary citizen from detecting the motions of the dollar is the same thing which prevents the child on a train from detecting the train's motion. To the child the fences seem to go scooting backward when it is the train carrying him forward. Even to the grown man the sun seems to move from east to west when it is the earth carrying him from west to east. So we, who ride the tide of dollars, think the price-shore is receding when it is the money-tide carrying us out to sea.

If money buys goods, goods buy money. If, therefore, overproduced goods mean cheap goods, why does not overproduced money mean cheap money? It is in fact cheap money and not dear goods from which we are suffering. When the abundance of money is sudden, as in war, we sometimes come to acknowledge it and call it by the name of "inflation". When the national output is below the productive capacity the policy should be to let money out. When production is at a maximum the outflow of money should be checked and if inflationary symptoms have appeared money should be withdrawn.

Now Mr. McKenna has set forth very distinctly the considerations that ought to weigh in a managed currency; that is, if we have a decreasing price-level, accompanied as it always is by business depression and unemployment, it should be the policy of statesmen to deliberately increase the supply of money in order to take up the slack, as it were, to get rid of unemployment, and to give encouragement to business. If, on the other hand, any inflationary symptoms appear, which will be indicated by an increasing price level, the proper policy would be to decrease the supply of money, and in that way prevent the ups and downs of business.
