The minister had no reasons to offer, but he concluded by informing the House that the Finance Act was working very well, and that being the case he seemed to imply that it was performing the chief function of a central bank in that it provided for discounting. Let me refer him to the gentleman who he admits is his best adviser, the Peputy Minister of Finance, and who told us in committee the other day that his best judgment was that we should get back to the gold basis. In other words, if we are to take the advice of the Deputy
11 p.m. Minister of Finance we shall do away with the Finance Act which the minister himself declares is working so admirably. It seems therefore that the Acting Minister of Finance and his chief adviser are somewhat at cross purposes so far as this particular question is concerned but even so that is no reason why this motion should be defeated. I desire now to deal briefly with the rather elaborate and detailed argument of the hon. member-

I rise to a point of order. I submit that the hon. member is not standing strictly by the rules .of procedure. As I understand it, there are two or three propositions before the House in the report which has been presented and the hon. member is discussing subjects which are removed from
any of the matters which are directly under consideration. I think the scope of the hon. gentleman's remarks should be circumscribed at least to what is relevant. I further object that the committee has no right to report on an order of reference in the manner in which it has been done. A report must first be made according to reference. Such is not the case here.

I am attempting to answer
the argument put forward by a representative of the government, and even if the minister was out of order I suppose the House will permit me nevertheless to reply to the points he has made. I do not say that my remarks are all strictly relevant, but a certain point having been brought forward by my opponents and admitted as argument leaves no other choice to me but to simite it.

There are two or three
propositions before the House with certain recommendations from the committee and if hon. gentlemen are to enter upon a discussion of questions relating to mining, commerce, soldier's civil re-establishment, and other matters of a like nature it seems to me that the debate is likely to get out of hand. The hon. member, I submit, should confine his remarks as closely as possible to a discussion of the report as it has been submitted, to the House. I am bringing this to your attention, Mr. Speaker, for the purpose solely of curbing hon. members like my hon. friend in their endeavours to make a speech which will go abroad rather than a speech which will be instructive to members of the House.

I am quite sure the hon.
gentleman will generally observe the rules. I must say that the discussion throughout the day has taken a very wide range, because the question before the House, if it were carried into effect would, from what I understand of it, affect the whole economy of our banking system. Therefore, naturally it opens very wide the discussion of the subject matter. I am quite sure, however, that hon. members in discussing the question at this late hour will confine themselves to the question before the House and not wander away too much.

I am glad to know that my
hon. friend is anxious about a speech that will go abroad in this matter.

I still rise to a point of
order. I am quite willing that my hon. friend should discuss the Bank Act, but I still persist in insisting that there are three or four questions before the House as a reference

Reserve Bank

from the Banking and Commerce committee. I am going to insist now, since my hon. friend gets sarcastic about the matter, that he be confined within the terms of those three propositions.

As I stated a moment
ago, this is a very important question which affects the whole economy of the banking system and which naturally goes to the very root of-our whole banking organization in this country. I cannot stop an hon. member who, I am sure, is quite willing and who desires to bring forward the best arguments to support his viewpoint. I am certain he will live up to the traditions of the House, that he must confine himself to the subject matter. So far, in my humble opinion, I do not see that he is out of order.
When my genial and loquacious friend interrupted me, I was coming to the argument of the hon, member for St. Lawrence-St. George.
No more loquacious than my hon. friend is.

I am sure that the hon.
member for St. Lawrence-St. George will be as genial in listening to my comment on his arguments as I was in taking his from him. He is, of course, always very genial and honourable in debate. On this occasion, however, he reminded me of a huge Atlantic liner surrounded by a very thick fog. There was a consciousness that there were dangers somewhere ahead, but she tooted the whistle and sailed on disregarding entirely the dangers that lay ahead. He emphasized the point that 22 members out of the 90 voted that this resolution be placed before parliament. The question is:	Where were the 90-the ninety
and nine that safely played cards or were somewhere else? I do not know. Twenty-two were on their job doing their duty.

Will my hon. friend allow me
to correct him? He knows it is unfair to members of the committee to say that. Several other committees were sitting at the same time, the committee on Private Bills, the committee on Railways, and we had all the difficulty in the world to get members present at our committee because other committees were sitting. It is unfair to say that hon. members were playing cards while the Banking and Commerce committee were sitting. They were busy on other committees of which they were members.

I certainly do not wish to
impute anything to any hon. member that I would not take to myself. But why did the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George raise that point?

If I remember well, he said
that only twenty-two voted for it against 7 who opposed it. That means twenty-nine member's out of ninety who are members of the committee voted on that question. But he did not insist on the suggestion that the other members were playing cards.
I do not insist on it either I did not say what they were doing. I mentioned a number of things which they might have been doing. I did not say that any hon. member was playing cards.

My hon. friend is unfair in
that reference.

I rise to a point of
order. I was a member of the Banking and Commerce committee, and it was not my privilege to vote on that question, but I deeply resent the unwarranted remark which the hon. member has just made. I was engaged on other committees. It is altogether out of keeping with the decorum which the hon. member usually keeps to make such an insinuation.

I have taken back twice
the insinuation that my hon. friends took from my remark, and I now take it back a third time. I would not think of imputing it to my hon. friend, although I would not say it was a great crime if he did play cards. As a matter of fact, I think we ought all to have a game after this discussion in order to get this contentious subject out of our heads. I did not mean to insinuate anything wrong to any hon. member. The twenty-two members were there, however, and this was the finding. They represented the committee at that time.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George charged, I think, that the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) was out of order in his discussion, because the only question for discussion was whether or not the reference should be enlarged, whereas the hon. member for West Calgary had argued as regards the whole banking system.
I did not say that the hon. member for West Calgary was out of order. He was not out of onder. We are always delighted to hear him.

I know he was not out of order, but my hon. friend used those words.

Reserve Bank
I never said so.

I was, however, glad that
my hon. friend came back to the point and said that it was a question on whether this parliament wTould authorize the committee to study the subject. If parliament is considering authorizing the committee to study the question, that opens up the whole question of the financial system of Canada and the United States and in any other country having a central bank of issue.

If my hon. friend will allow
me-

If the hon. members wish
me to finish anywhere this side of one o'clock, they had better let me go on. I do not object to questions, but I have a great deal of sympathy with hon. members who have to listen to me.

If my hon. friend will allow
me, he will agree to the fact that the report of the committee was obtained on a "snap" vote, on a vote which was taken at a moment when only 29 members out of 90 were present in the committee, the other members being busy elsewhere.

I do not know whether
it was a "snap" vote or not. I certainly do know there was not much snap shown by my hon. friend in bringing the recommendation before the House. In this regard it took my hon. friend about four weeks to "snap." I am not concerned about the nature of the vote. I had nothing to do with that, neither had this House. It was reported as a majority vote, and that is all we have to do with it.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George apparently assumed that we wanted to transplant the American banking system into Canada merely because we asked to be allowed to consider the establishment of some type of central reserve bank. Now, it might not at all be fatal to transplant the American financial system over here. I am not sure about that. I think it is absurd to claim that a system which functions to serve a hundred million people could not serve nine million. But that is not really the argument. The argument is that we are seeking to consider some type, and all types for that matter, of a central banking system to see whether we can devise one that will be suitable to this country. That is the issue. But my hon. friend went on to describe in detail the functions of a bank. As he described them they are briefly these:	First, to issue
notes; second, to take deposits; third, to give elasticity of circulation; fourth, to give
elasticity of credits. If these were the functions of a bank, our system performs them very well. That is to say, our banks issue notes-and they do it gladly; they take deposits-and sometimes they keep them; they certainly have great elasticity of circulation1- when they want to; and they have great elasticity of credits- when it suits them; and they can contract it just as easily. Yes, if that constitutes the functions of a banking system, I agree with my hon. friend that we do not need any central reserve bank to facilitate these functions. But he might just as well have described a ship as being something that functions: first, to exhibit a figurehead; second, to be driven by steam; third, to be guided by a rudder; and fourth, to toot a whistle! That is a parallel description of my hon. friend's argument respecting the banking system. These things mentioned by him do not constitute the functions of a bank, they constitute the phases of a function. The main function of a banking system was entirely missed by my hon. friend. I repeat, if these were the functions of a bank, I would consider the introduction of a central reserve bank of no assistance to do these things, because they are very well done already.
The hon. member contended that the central banking system of the United States is entirely unsuited for Canada. He has so decided already. Then he points to the report of Mr. Skelton Williams and enumerates for us the phases of a central banking system. Then he tells us that we already have that system in Canada. After he has said that that system is entirely unsuited to Canada, he turns around and proves that we have every phase of it now! I cannot follow my hon. friend's reasoning.

Let my hon. friend be
fair.
Yes.

Really he is acting as a
contortionist. He is very amusing, in fact he is making a burlesque of the subject, but this is a serious debate.

I am glad to be informed
by my hon. friend that he was not serious when he was speaking; I really did think so, and was trying to answer his argument in the same tone in which I assumed it was presented. If he was not serious, then I do not need to say any more about it. Let me hasten to conclude. All we are asking in this resolution is that parliament permit the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce to study this question. Are my hon. friends
Reserve Bank

afraid of what such a study may bring forth? If it should reveal that a central banking system is as impracticable, as dangerous, as inadequate as horn, members on the other side of the House have said it is, then surely we will not attempt to introduce it, and there can come nothing but good from seeking information. All we are asking is that the select standing committee be authorized to seek information. I trust that such authority will be given.
You have it.

Mr. Speaker, I would point out to the House the importance of really trying to ascertain what is the opinion of hon. members as to what ought to be done having regard to the absolute essentiality of some policy, some direction from the government. Surely the government now see what the result of a discussion at large is upon this matter. They see the different views presented-and many of them are reasonable-and they also see the conflict of some of those views. For example, on the one hand they see that it is the considered opinion of hon. gentlemen, supported by authority, that dear goods simply means cheap money; on the other hand, they are told, also supported by authority, that the answer to low prices and poor business is merely more money-cheap money. They see that we can get from financial authorities, from financial writers at any rate, a circle that will take this government back to just where it started. Surely the country is entitled to at least a little bit of decision from the government, for after all this is governmental business, this is not a merely idle academic debate. On May 21 this decision was arrived at; on July 2 the House gets an opportunity of debating it. What an idle opportunity it is! I do not like to see the House attempting idle things. What would happen if this resolution is today adopted? Does anyone think that in the expiring days of this session the question can be studied and settled? We all know it is nonsense to think so; it cannot be done. Hon. gentlemen wanted a discussion. They no doubt had a right to that discussion under the arrangement come to. But why did not the discussion take place when we could have done something useful with it?

Will my hon. friend allow
me a correction? Even if this motion had been discussed on May 21, the Banking and Commerce committee could not have considered a study of the question. The committee have sat for about twenty-three days, 
and they still have twenty-two more resolutions to consider before they can come to this question, even if it be referred to them by the House.
Well, Mr. Speaker, perhaps the committee might have thought this would be more important than some of the other twenty-two resolutions.
I do not believe it.

It may be that the committee are trying to do so much themselves to-day that nothing will be done in regard to this resolution. But it is only a matter of regret, if we spread ourselves out so thin as to try to cover the whole universe. It is perfectly idle to say that anything can be done to-day. I am going to vote against the report because I do not believe in parliament doing idle things. What will be the effect of the vote? To say that during the few days that remain to us among twenty-two other resolutions this resolution may be considered is tantamount to admitting the futility of instructing the committee, for the committee ceases just as soon as this House ceases.
When is it going to cease?

Well, I hope we are not going to stay here indefinitely and permanently. That is the last thing in the world that the country wants. I think a lot of people in the country have the idea that they are getting worse legislation from this House than they would have got if there were no House at all, and that we would be pleasing them best if we got away just as soon as we could. I am inclined to believe that that is what the general public think. Nevertheless these are important questions and questions which should be considered when there is opportunity to consider them. I doubt very much whether this matter is in order at all. I did not want to raise the point until the discussion was over because I wanted my hon. friends to have the opportunity of placing their views before the House. But the report on this question of inspection is in, and I think as a matter of order that the instructions are now discharged and if anything is to be done it must be a new committal to the committee. We might just as reasonably ask that we should have another Speech from the Throne.

Mr. Speaker, I was paired with the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson). While I am not in a position to say how he would have voted on the question, had I voted I would have voted against the recommendation of the committee.

Mr. Speaker, it was my intention to-night, in accordance with notice given, to move that the first report of the select standing committee to supervise the Official Report of Debates be concurred in. But when this motion was brought up the other day and the unanimous consent of the House was asked, the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) objected. I see that the right hon. gentleman is not in his seat at the moment. I do not know whether he is in the building or not, but if he is not here I would defer until tomorrow the presentation of the motion and substitute therefor a motion which merely covers the last part of the report, to which the right hon. leader of the opposition is quite agreeable. I therefore move, seconded by Mr. Logan:
That the following questions he referred to the select standing committee on Debates for the purpose of considering the same and reporting their opinion thereon to the House, viz:-
1.	Whether Hansard should be a record of debates only, containing such items of the proceedings of the House as may be necessary to make the report of the debates intelligible, or whether it should contain all the proceedings of the House as well as the record of debates.
2.	Whether it is desirable, in the interests of economy of time, labour and expense, that the report of the debates in Hansard should be limited to such speeches as may ibe delivered when Mr. Speaker is in the dhair, with or without a brief report of the proceedings in committee.
3.	Whether it is desirable to make Hansard an official record of all the proceedings of the House of Commons, as well as a record of the debates.
I understand that even to move this motion I would have to have unanimous consent, but I already have the consent of the hon. leader of the opposition.
Motion agreed to.

POST OFFICE EMPLOYEES Mr. CHURCH:
1.	What amount of money has been spent by the government to test the validity of the Industrial Disputes Act in the law courts to date in order to compel the appointment of a board of conciliation for the Hydro-electric employees at Toronto, and has any appeal been taken, or to be taken, to the Privy Council on the subject?
2.	Has the government refused a similar board of conciliation to the Post Office employees as not coming within the act?
3.	What conciliation was used by the government, if any, to adjust the Post Office strike?
Hon, Mr. MURDOCK:
1.	The government did not undertake to test the validity of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act in the law courts.
The facts as understood are that on the advice of the member of parliament for North Toronto and others, the Toronto Hydro-Electric Commission protested the formation of a Board of Investigation, which had been applied for June 25 and established July 24, 1923, and later secured an injunction from Mr. Justice Orde to restrain the board from sitting.
Later Mr. Justice Mowat disagreed with the decision of Mr. Justice Orde, but instructed1 that the case be carried to the Appeal Court of Ontario which later, by a judgment [Mr. Murdock.)
of four to one, decided that the Toronto Hydro-Electric Commission and Mr. Justice Orde were in error in the injunction sought and granted.
It is understood that an appeal from the decision of the Appeal Court of Ontario which sustained the action of the department in forming a board, has been taken to the Privy Council. In the meantime the board has not been permitted to function.
The cost of protecting the Department of Labour's rights under the conditions referred to above has to date been 87,297.05, which amount in whole or in part may be salvaged as the latest decision assesses costs against the Toronto Hydro-Electric Commission.
2.	No application for a board was received by the Registrar of Boards of Conciliation.
The Minister of Labour advised certain persons inquiring, that a Board of Investigation would not foe granted to determine whether Post Office employees' salaries, established by the Civil Service Commission and approved by the Governor-in-Council, in accordance with the law, should or should not be revised.
It is definitely held that government employees do not, and were not, intended to come within the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, but that the compensation of civil servants is, under the law, specifically established by a separate commission.
3.	Early in the month of April 1924, members of the government' on several occasions covering a period of two weeks or more met with officers of the Postal Workers Federation on account of the threatened strike of postal workers to be made effective about April 15, unless prior to that date the salaries of postal workers had been dealt with and revised by the Civil Service Commission. The government also intimated to the Civil Service Commission the desirability of proceeding as promptly as possible to revise the salaries of all of the branches of the government service, giving first consideration to the revision of the postal workers salaries.
These matters were also discussed with the government Board of Audit. Later the Civil Service Commission presented to the government its proposed revision of postal workers salaries, and that revision appearing to be less acceptable than proposals for salary revision which had been made by Post Office Department officials, the proposed revision of the Civil Service Commission was referred back to that body with a request that further consideration be given to the various representations that had been made, and that

Questions
additional opportunity be given to the representatives of postal workers and department officers to present their respective views or claims to the Civil Service Commission. The Board of Audit were also requested to give careful consideration to the salary revision for postal workers, and later the Board of Audit made known to the government its recommendations as to salary revision, which was found to be in respect to some fifteen classifications slightly higher or better than those which had been proposed by the Civil Service Commission.
The government therefore requested that the Civil Service Commission give further consideration to this matter, and for that purpose had before them the Civil Service Commission and the Board of Audit.
On June 9 the Governor in Council gave consideration to the Civil Service Commission's final report to the government on postal workers' salary revision, which was the third report to the government that had been made by the Civil Service Commission in this matter, although there was no difference in the rates of compensation proposed in either of the three reports.
On the same date a copy of the Civil Service Commission's report, as approved by the Governor in Council, was handed to the officers of the Postal Workers Federation.
No further word or representations were received from officers of the Postal Workers Federation until the morning of June 17, when a telegram dated June 16 was received by the Minister of Labour from Mr. G. R. Jackson, President -of the Postal Workers Federation reading:
Postal situation developing more serious parliament can and should immediately right a wrong. Let me hear from you.
Reply was within the hour sent to Mr. Jackson as follows:
Your telegram of last evening will be brought before government to-day.
And on the same day, June 17, the matter was discussed by the government, and suggestion made that the Minister of Labour should communicate with the Postal Workers committee at Toronto to suggest that they come to Ottawa for conference with members of the government.
On the afternoon of June 17, the Minister of Labour by long distance telephone suggested to Chairman G. R. Jackson, of the Postal Workers Federation that the committee should come to Ottawa, and on that evening the committee representing the postal workers left Toronto, arriving in Otttawa on the morning of June 18.
251 i
On June 18, the postal workers committee were in the Minister of Labour's office from about 10.40 a.m. until 1 p.m. discussing with four members of the government the conditions of dissatisfaction said to exist and the objections filed by the postal workers against the revision of salaries that had been given to the committee on June 9.
It was discovered at this conference that the Postal Workers Federation had before leaving Toronto on the evening of June 17 authorized a Dominion-wide strike of all postal workers to become effective as of 5 p.m. on the evening of June 18.
At 1 p.m. on June 18, the conference in the Minister of Labour's office adjourned to permit the four members of the cabinet to discuss in council the situation as it had developed, and at 3.10 p.m. on June 18 the conference between the postal workers and members of the cabinet again met in the Minister of Labour's office, and the postal workers were given the following letter:
June 18, 1924.
Mr. J. E. Archer,
Secretary, Canadian Federation of Postal Employees,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Sir,
This acknowledges receipt of a copy of your letter of even date addressed to the Right Honourable the Prime Minister advising him that:
"Acting on the wishes of the membership of the organizations concerned, as expressed in a Dominionwide ballot, a general strike in the Postal Service has been called to commence at five o'clock this afternoon." After discussion of this matter with the government, I am authorized to state that we regret the decision arrived at by your committee, and it is a matter of additional regret that your committee have not prior to this date officially indicated to the government your dissatisfaction with the recent salary revision for postal workers as authorized by the Civil Service Commission and the government.
Since the receipt of your letter of even date, a su!b-committee of the cabinet has had the opportunity of discussing these matters at some length with your committee and have heard the views of your committee that further consideration should be given to the claims of the postal employees by the government.
In connection with this matter the Prime Minister in parliament yesterday stated as follows:
"We are prepared, when the Civil Service Commission has submitted its report upon the salaries of the entire civil service, to consider that report carefully in the light of all the material which we have before us and to make to parliament, if we think it advisable so to do, recommendations supplementing those which are contained in the report of the Civil Service Commission. But we do not feel that we are in a position to make any recommendations to parliament at the present time with respect to the postal employees; and I hope that the employees of the Post Office Department will see that the position which the government is taking is one which is in the interests of the entire civil service of the country and in the interests of the taxpayers as wefll."
We also in discussion of this date learned of the dissatisfaction of the postal employees due to the
Questions

fact that in certain cases the present salary plus 1924 bonus was higher than certain rates proposed by the Civil Service Commission for the same class of employees, and I am authorized to state that in the case of employees whose revised rates, as determined by the Civil Service Commission are less than the former rate plus 1924-25 bonus, such bonus shall oe continued until salary revision for the entire service has been consummated.
I am further authorized to say that in carrying out the plan and action proposed by the Prime Minister in the above quoted paragraph, that the government policy is that when the Civil Service Commission has submitted its report upon the salaries for the entire civil service, that opportunity will be given to the representatives of the employees in the Postal Department or in other departments of the government who have objections to file against salary revision proposed by the commission to fully present their views to a sub-committee of the government and to discuss such matters of differences as fully as may be necessary to ensure a thorough understanding, and, it is hoped a final and satisfactory agreement on the points in dispute.
I trust that your committee will at once take the necessary action to see that continuous operation of the Postal Service is maintained.
Charles Stewart,
Acting Postmaster General.
At 4 p.m. on June 18, members of the government withdrew from the Minister of Labour's office, leaving the postal workers committee in conference to determine their further action, and at 4.45 p.m. the Minister of Labour rapped on the door and advised the postal workers committee that 5 o'clock was only fifteen minutes distant and that some decision should be made as to whether the strike ordered for 5 p.m. was or was not to take place.
At 4.56 p.m. the postal workers agreed that the strike order for 5 p.m. that date would be set back for 24 hours, and at once by long distance telephone and otherwise, from the Minister of Labour's office, the committee undertook to advise their local representatives at Toronto and elsewhere that the postponement of the strike order had been determined upon by the general committee at Ottawa.
During the evening of June 18 for two or three hours the postal workers committee were in the office of the Acting Postmaster General at the House of Commons with members of the government endeavouring to set back for 24 hours the strike, which had in many places, as a result of previous orders given, taken effect in some towns and cities of Ontario and at other points.
On the evening of June 18 the postal workers' committee left for Toronto, and during the next day efforts were still made by the government to secure an adherence to the understandings reached the previous day that the strike would be held in abeyance for 24 hours.

About 4.30 p.m. on the afternoon of June 19 the Minister of Labour was called by long distance phone from Toronto by Mr. J. E. Archer, who advised that he had resigned his position as secretary of the Postal Workers' Federation, and that he was returning at once to Hamilton to insist that the postal workers at that point should return to duty and permit the government to carry out the understanding and proposals that had been made in letter of the previous day which had been addressed to him as Secretary of the Postal Workers Federation, the result being that shortly thereafter Hamilton postal workers returned to duty, although during the time they had been out on strike some 130 men had been employed in the postal service.
Before the postal workers committee left Ottawa they had been advised by the Acting Postmaster General that as they had earnestly endeavoured to set back the strike for 24 hours it would not be held that the strike was in effect until the committee definitely advised him that such was the case.
Late on the evening of June 19 advice was received from Mr. G. R. Jackson, President of the Postal Workers Federation that a strike of postal employees had been authorized and made effective as of 5 p.m. on the 19th, although as a matter of fact the strike had been effective in Toronto and at some other points for 24 hours prior to that time.
Efforts at conciliation then ceased, as it became then a question of determining whether the government or striking postal employees were in charge of the mail facilities.

subtopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916

speechtext:
Hon. J. A. ROBB (Acting Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to provide, that the Business Profits War Tax Act, 1916, and amendments, shall be construed and have effect and be deemed to have had effect since its enactment without lapse or interruption as if section twenty-six thereof when first enacted had provided as follows:-
" The provisions of section three of this act shall not continue in force after the thirty-first day of December, one thousand nine hundred and twenty; and anything enacted inconsistent therewith shall be deemed to have been superseded, amended or repealed, as the circumstances may require, and all taxes, interest and penalties payable under the said act and amendments shall remain a tax owning to His Majesty until fully paid and satisfied.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Robb thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 219, respecting the Business Profits War Tax Act, 1916.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, considered in committee, and reported.
